item.title: Optimism Is Not a Personality Trait, It's an Explanatory Style You Can Train
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.description: Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself, but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.
item.content:encoded:
Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself, but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.

Seligman himself walks through the full chain from learned helplessness to learned optimism, and in the back half treats agency as a civilisational variable to be quantified — a rare angle.

9:36 The dog doesn't run, and it isn't because it never learned to run
In Solomon's lab, on day one the dog was strapped into a hammock and given Pavlovian shocks it could not escape no matter what it did; on day two it was placed in a shuttle box where running to the other side would switch off the shock, and the dog just lay there. Seligman's reading: what the animal actually learned was not "the tone predicts a shock" but "nothing I do matters." That interpretation collided head-on with behaviourism at the time, because it required the animal to be a cognitive subject capable of thinking and of integrating experience across time.

13:50 People can be taught to give up by noise too
Hiroto moved the same design onto humans: on day one, headphones playing an unpleasant noise, with one group unable to switch it off no matter what they pressed and another group able to stop it with a button. On day two they were given a four-foot "human shuttle box" — hand on one side, the noise sounds; move it to the other side, it stops. People who had been through uncontrollable noise the day before left their hand sitting in the box. Seligman stresses that the variable doing the work is not the trauma itself but whether there was control over the trauma — and they ran control experiments on exactly this point.

19:00 Helplessness became the model for depression
In 1970 depression was not yet a diagnostic category; there was only "manic-depressive illness." By 1975 the American Psychiatric Association's DSM had for the first time split out "unipolar depression," listing nine symptoms: passivity, cognitive difficulty, sadness, anxiety, sleep problems, food losing its taste, numbness, loss of pleasure, thoughts of death. Seligman compared the nine symptoms against the learned-helplessness literature that had accumulated by then and found that eight of them could be reproduced in the lab; the only one missing was thoughts of death — presumably because the experiments used noise rather than something more severe. The model went on to become the dominant model of depression, and the drugs that could break helplessness in the lab became the mainstream antidepressants.

22:19 Five out of eight give up; a third never do
Across the whole helplessness literature the effect is statistical: on average five out of eight people, or eight rats, become helpless, and roughly a third do not. From the 1970s onward Seligman kept asking what was different about that third, and it became the turning point of his career. The answer landed on explanatory style: people who explain bad events as permanent ("I'm stupid"), pervasive ("I'm unlovable"), and their own fault become helpless; people who explain them as temporary, local, and not their fault recover quickly.

26:50 West Point's first week already predicts who drops out
The first six weeks after entering West Point are called Beast Barracks: woken at four in the morning to run ten miles, systematically put through the wringer, with the stated purpose being to "break them," and roughly a third of candidates quit. Seligman's team measured explanatory style on day one, and the ones who dropped out were the pessimists. The same pattern shows up in college grades (optimists outperform their talent, pessimists underperform it) and in insurance sales: MetLife lost 50% of new hires within a year and 90% within four years; they hired 140 "special forces" whose optimism-scale scores were off the charts, and this cohort outsold the whole company and still had 75% on the job after four years, while the ordinary group was down to 10%.

34:17 Agency breaks down into three beliefs
Seligman defines agency as the opposite of learned helplessness, made up of three parts: efficacy, the belief that you can accomplish a specific goal right here and now; optimism, the belief that you can accomplish it not only now but in the future and the further future; and imagination, the range of possible goals you can picture — the wider the range, the stronger the agency. Full agency is: I can do it now, I can do it later, and I can innovate across many different situations.

36:22 The axial age's answer may have been "I can do it"
Between 1000 and 500 BCE, Greece, the Hebrew world, China, India and Persia all underwent upheaval: the Buddha, Confucius and Socrates appeared, and technology, medicine, art, literature and the first political freedoms all erupted together. Seligman's hypothesis is that over those five centuries humanity discovered the concept of agency. The evidence is vocabulary: in the Iliad, Achilles does not decide to act on his own — Athena tells him to act; a hundred years later, in the Odyssey, Odysseus is already a wily, resourceful man who makes his own decisions, and the gods begin to exit the stage. By 500 BCE, every culture had produced a large vocabulary of human agency.

38:30 In the Old Testament, the verbs God commands with are dwindling
Seligman took the entire Old Testament and counted agency verbs: broadly, in the Pentateuch God commands and people obey, with only a few exceptions such as "choose life"; the further you go, into the Prophets and the Writings, the more words for human agency appear and the fewer for divine agency. You can now have AI score each book for agency, and plotted by date it comes out linear — from the Pentateuch to the Babylonian exile around 300 BCE, agency increases, and it correlates linearly with human innovation, population, living standards, political freedom and technology.

item.title: Apple Puts a New CEO on Stage, but the AI Answer Isn't There Yet
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果把新-ceo-推上台-但-ai-的答案还没找到/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果把新-ceo-推上台-但-ai-的答案还没找到/
item.description: The iPhone Duo is the coolest Apple product in a decade, and it was unveiled by a CEO two weeks into the job — a deliberate arrangement so the new CEO gets credit for an entire new product cycle, rather than letting Cook pick the fruit at the end of his tenure.
item.content:encoded:
The iPhone Duo is the coolest Apple product in a decade, and it was unveiled by a CEO two weeks into the job — a deliberate arrangement so the new CEO gets credit for an entire new product cycle, rather than letting Cook pick the fruit at the end of his tenure.

High information density: Mark Gurman walks through Apple's executive overhaul, its stalled AI strategy, and the privacy-versus-smart-glasses dilemma, item by item. For anyone tracking Apple's organization and product roadmap.

5:00 Ternus and Cook have completely different management styles
Gurman's comparison, from people inside: you bring an idea to Tim Cook and he keeps probing, and in many cases won't give you a single decision — it's collective, collaborative decision-making; you go to John Ternus and he makes a decision, he has an opinion — you may hate the opinion, you may completely disagree with it, but he has one. That's the biggest difference between the two. The first thing Ternus did on taking over was put out his own view on AI: the intelligent personal hub. Gurman says whether or not you agree with the view, at least they finally have a clear narrative, whereas Apple's AI has been a mishmash with no strong narrative since Apple Intelligence launched at WWDC 2024.

8:08 The September 2026 event shipped no new AI features at all
Gurman points out a sharp fact: Apple held a major product event in September 2026 and did not introduce a single notable new AI feature. The first 15 minutes of the keynote were just a recap and re-narrativization of the past two years of Apple Intelligence. Apple has no AI-centric device, so it has to prop up the iPhone as their AI device, because there is no alternative. But once there's a killer device, the whole narrative changes. Gurman says this isn't a criticism — if he ran the company he'd sell what he had too — but Apple is a narrative-, VR- and marketing-driven company, and this time they played it very safe.

14:14 Cook could have closed out with the iPhone Duo, but he didn't
Gurman makes the key point: Apple's typical CEO transitions happen in mid-October, mid-April or on January 1. Letting Ternus launch the iPhone Duo, and launch the entire new product roadmap, is a specific decision. This hardware has been in the oven for five to ten years because of development cycles and R&D. Cook could have waited until after the iPhone Duo launch to hand over, keeping the credit for himself, but he chose to make Ternus the face of this new product era. Gurman's read: if Cook was going to step down within three years anyway, better to do it now, let Ternus take all the credit, and draw a clear line between the old era and the new.

19:28 Apple's executive overhaul was staged step by step over five years
Gurman reconstructs the timeline: in 2023 Cook started saying at every executive meeting that ‘we have to take succession seriously.’ At that point the top ranks either had $500 million in the bank or were billionaires, and this era was going to age out fast. So they made a plan and went one by one: at the end of 2024 CFO Luca Maestri retired, Kevin Parekh took over; in 2025 COO Jeff Williams retired, his deputy Sabih Khan took over; in 2026 general counsel Kate Adams retired, and Jennifer Newstead was poached from Meta; at the end of 2026, Cook handed over to Ternus. Gurman calls this retention strategy ‘Hotel California’ — you never want to leave. Cook stays on as executive chairman, the general counsel stays six to nine more months to handle government affairs, and after stepping down as COO Jeff Williams stayed three or four more months overseeing design, watch and health teams.

23:33 Schiller left because he didn't want to squeeze developers for more money
Gurman's reporting shows Phil Schiller gave up his two remaining responsibilities, the App Store and Apple events, partly because of age and family, but also because of a roadmap split in the new era: Eddy Cue now firmly controls all of Apple's services, and Ternus is close to Eddy Cue, and they're looking for new ways to make more money from the App Store — more ad slots, more subscription opportunities, and over the next few years the App Store will be redesigned around AI and Siri AI. Schiller has always thought Apple squeezes developers too hard, and he thinks regulators are still watching Apple closely and developers are still unhappy, and he wanted to keep a bit of distance in this new era. Gurman stresses there was no big blowup between Schiller and Cue or Ternus — it was just a stack of considerations that naturally arrived at the moment to exit.

31:52 Failing to keep young people is why Apple didn't see AI
Gurman draws a direct line from talent retention to the AI misstep: Eddy Cue has been at Apple nearly forty years, the people under him want to succeed him but know he'll never leave, so they go elsewhere for bigger opportunities, and Apple keeps losing good people at the VP level. Gurman argues that without a bench of younger replacements with fresh, disruptive ideas, Apple in some ways failed to see what AI was. He brings up the Cook Doctrine — Tim Cook often says Apple has to own and control every foundational technology that goes into the phone, which is Apple's paranoia about being tied to Intel for so long. But they can't see a path to owning and controlling AI, because the investment is too big, and they'd just burned a pile of money on the car.

33:55 Apple says it will build its own models, but Gurman sees no evidence
Gurman says the thinking inside Apple has always been: the Google partnership is just a stopgap until we can build our own models from scratch. But he also says he has seen no evidence that Apple is pushing Plan A again — no evidence they're heads-down building new Apple first-party models from scratch, no evidence they're out doing big AI acquisitions, no evidence they're willing to pay AI researchers the kind of massive packages Meta, Google, Anthropic and OpenAI pay. Right now it feels stalled: they want to see how the Google deal and third-party partnerships play out over the next few months, see the Anthropic and OpenAI IPOs, see the news on AI safety, and maybe decide a direction in six months.

48:19 The watch's all-day listening feature is a problem Apple created itself
Gurman reacted strongly to the watchOS 27 all-day listening transcription feature: ‘I can't believe they did this.’ The feature just listens, and a double tap shows a transcript of the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you, without their permission. Gurman says Apple knows the next generation of AI-driven user interfaces needs some amount of ambient capture — whether it's hearing you talk or seeing the world around you — but they haven't solved the social privacy layer. They have white papers on how to solve technical database privacy, they have private cloud compute, they encrypt data and don't store it, but Gurman thinks none of that overcomes the social privacy problem. Apple didn't spend enough time in the keynote unpacking this feature, and he thinks it was launched badly.

item.title: The Real Bottleneck in the Treasury Market: Not Size, but Not Enough Intermediaries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-macromusings-美债市场真正的瓶颈-不是规模-是中间商不够用了/

item.description: Primary dealer balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers gave way to high-frequency traders — but those traders collectively retreated in March 2020. That is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.
item.content:encoded:
Primary dealer balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers gave way to high-frequency traders — but those traders collectively retreated in March 2020. That is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.

A front-line New York Fed operator explains Treasury market structure, with empirical data from two 2025 papers and the latest TBAC developments. High information density.

11:26 The Treasury market is so big it has to attract new buyers
Golay gives the scale: CBO counts $30 trillion in outstanding Treasuries at the end of 2025, and projects another $26 to $27 trillion over the next decade. The market splits into two parts — the cash market (buying and selling Treasuries directly, some through inter-dealer broker electronic trading, some dealer-to-client) and the repo market (borrowing against Treasuries as collateral, mostly intermediated by dealers). A market this large and growing necessarily has to attract different types of investors, including price-sensitive high-frequency traders and hedge funds.

14:31 High-frequency traders went from zero to the main force in electronic markets
Golay calls these firms principal trading firms (PTFs), mostly running high-frequency strategies and trading on electronic platforms. Twenty years ago they were not in the Treasury market at all; today they may account for the majority of trading in the electronic cash market. The turning point was the 2014 flash rally — yields swung sharply and no one could explain why, which is when the official sector began to truly understand how PTFs had grown in electronic markets, and which also sparked the IAWG's work to study market structure and obtain better data.

16:33 Primary dealer balance sheets have not kept up with the growth in outstanding Treasuries
Golay cites a chart from a Darrell Duffie paper: the size of primary dealer balance sheets devoted to intermediating Treasuries has simply not kept pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Part of the reason is post-2008 reforms, and part is that the growth in outstanding debt itself has been too fast. The result is that the market has had to attract more price-sensitive types of investors. She also corrects a common impression: it is not that PTFs always retreat during volatility — in other volatile periods the official sector has observed PTFs increasing their activity; but in March 2020, everyone retreated.

19:42 The essence of all-to-all is bypassing dealer matching
All-to-all trading is literally that: any participant in the Treasury market can trade with any other participant. That is nothing new in the equity market, but the Treasury market is largely over-the-counter and dealer-intermediated, so it is not. Golay points out that entering the March 2020 crisis, dealers already had a lot of Treasuries piled up on their balance sheets, and when the wave of selling hit there was no intermediation capacity left. If you could find a counterparty to match with without going through a dealer, that might ease things. But she says plainly that at the time most people were selling, and it is hard to imagine all-to-all perfectly solving that situation — it is just that every incremental improvement helps.

22:51 All-to-all is stuck on the absence of counterparty matching
One of the paper's core findings: in the off-the-run market, if you look at a 15-minute window, almost no one wants to buy the same off-the-run security you want to sell. Stretch the window to a day, and the match rate rises to 60% to 70%. Golay mentions possible directions for innovation, such as an end-of-day batch auction, and some institutions already have that capability. But to date, no case in this area has really gotten off the ground successfully. She also notes that expanding central clearing could push the transition to all-to-all, because you would not need to establish bilateral clearing arrangements with every counterparty — you would only need to connect to a central counterparty.

29:06 Off-the-run is 97% of outstanding debt, yet a liquidity backwater
Off-the-run refers to older Treasuries, ranging from those issued three months ago to 29- and 30-year bonds, and accounts for about 97% of outstanding Treasuries. The selling in the March 2020 dash for cash was mainly off-the-run, and the off-the-run market is dealer-intermediated, with no all-to-all. Golay and colleagues at the Board of Governors and the New York Fed did empirical work using TRACE data collected by FINRA, in which transaction-level data is visible only to the official sector. The conclusion: the older the Treasury, the worse its liquidity — larger price impact, lower volume, wider bid-ask spreads.

31:15 The cheapest to deliver can revive liquidity
Another finding of the paper: when an off-the-run Treasury becomes the cheapest to deliver into a Treasury futures contract, its liquidity is better than that of comparable off-the-run securities. This suggests the off-the-run problem is partly about trading activity itself — with trading activity, liquidity improves; without it, liquidity deteriorates. On policy implications, Golay mentions that Treasury buybacks can create trading activity around off-the-run securities and improve liquidity; central clearing makes clearing smoother; and as for reducing the number of issuance dates and making individual issues larger, the paper reaches no conclusion, because investors also like the finer granularity of monthly issuance.

36:33 TBAC put the brakes on expanding transparency
At a recent TBAC meeting, a member suggested expanding transparency around Treasury trading data: there is already market-wide aggregate statistics, as well as transaction-level data for on-the-run securities; the suggestion was to consider publishing transaction-level data for Treasury bills, and more frequent on-the-run data. But TBAC expressed caution about expanding transparency in other areas, including the off-the-run and TIPS markets. Golay says this is interesting, because data transparency is precisely the focus of the IAWG's recent work and was listed as a priority in 2021. She personally thinks a small incremental increase in transparency would be beneficial, but understands that in less liquid markets, releasing too much information can make intermediation very difficult.

item.title: Stanford Has a Secret Course That Teaches 12 People How to Extract Value From Other Humans
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-grayarea-斯坦福有一门秘密课程-教12个人如何从他人身上提取价值/

item.category: The Gray Area with Sean Illing
item.description: The course never appears in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO about extracting value from people. The students lie, the author says, not by accident but because the machine has rewarded it for years.
item.content:encoded:
The course never appears in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO about extracting value from people. The students lie, the author says, not by accident but because the machine has rewarded it for years.

This is not a generic Silicon Valley critique — it is a specific investigation with course names, dollar figures and named people; if you care about early-stage investing and talent pipelines, the detail density is high.

5:12 You can raise hundreds of thousands before you have a company
Pre-idea funding was the newest layer of the game when Theo arrived on campus: give an 18-year-old who just showed up hundreds of thousands, even millions, of dollars, sign a one-page SAFE check, agree that "when you start a company someday, come back to us" — and otherwise the money never has to be repaid. For a VC that's pocket change; they don't actually believe in these hyped-up teenagers, and they don't need you personally to succeed — they just need one overnight sensation. Meanwhile students are encouraged to make enormous promises and then discover again and again that nobody follows up: you can lie and face no consequences.

13:22 The secret course teaches extracting value
Stanford has a course that never appears in the catalog, called How to Rule the World, taught by a Silicon Valley CEO who has packaged himself as a professor. It admits only 12 students a year, and merely knowing it exists is a status marker. Its central assignment is extracting value from people, with a strong flavor of the ends justifying the means. One woman Theo interviewed said the course taught her how to lie to VCs to raise money — she went on to raise millions, drop out of Stanford, and this despite having already been caught cheating in a computer science class; months later she released a glossy launch video for a technology that didn't exist, and Silicon Valley cheered her on anyway, installed her in a mansion, and invited her back to Stanford to speak.

26:46 Ethics isn't a premise; getting caught is what counts
During ethics week in the intro computer science course, the professor presented the case of a software defect that killed four people in a radiotherapy device, and the TA asked who in the room cared about ethics — Theo was the only one who raised his hand. Weeks later a classmate told him he was taking a business ethics course, and "we're all just there to figure out how they got caught." He didn't sense that these people felt any need to pretend to care; when Sam Bankman-Fried was under house arrest at the house on the Stanford campus where he grew up, students made pilgrimages, threw parties themed around him, and said they wanted to replicate his success minus the final fall. A colleague's summary of the money that mysteriously vanished at Tree Hacks: it's all just a little bit of fraud.

38:01 The real reason the president fell wasn't the data
Board members who removed Marc Tessier-Lavigne later told Theo that one of their heaviest reasons was his posture — a highly aggressive public stance when challenged, deny, deny, deny, plus the threatening letters sent by the lawyer he hired, Steve Neal, which embarrassed the university. Theo found no evidence that Tessier-Lavigne himself falsified data: the problem lay in the labs he oversaw, where subordinates fabricated results in papers he co-authored, including the 2009 paper claiming to have found the cause of Alzheimer's, while internal company results before publication showed its central finding was "at best unreliable." He was asked to retract and refused, dragging it out for a decade. What drove him out was image management, not the data.

39:01 Four days after being ousted, the mansion closed
Four days after the board unanimously removed him, Tessier-Lavigne closed on a 7,600-square-foot mansion in "America's most expensive zip code," valued at over $10 million; eight months later he announced he had raised $1 billion for a new company doing AI biotech. Of the two VCs that led the round, an investor at one messaged Theo two months later to rib him about it, followed by a winking emoji; an investor at the other offered him money to start a company. Theo says it's the most Silicon Valley thing you could imagine: everything can be monetized, even taking down a university president turns into an invitation.

45:44 Duck syndrome: paddling like mad under the surface
Duck syndrome is a term Stanford coined itself: students glide across the surface like ducks, making everything look effortless, while underneath their legs paddle furiously just to stay afloat. Katie Meyer was its best illustration — captain of the women's soccer team, an NCAA champion, headed to law school, didn't drink, didn't smoke, didn't speed. Months before graduation, late on a Friday night, after every student support office had closed, she received a letter: because six months earlier she had spilled coffee on a football player (she said it was an accident, he said it was deliberate), her degree was suspended. That night she took her own life. Twelve schools later paid tribute to her; Stanford was not among them. The women's soccer team she had just led held a mental health night and never mentioned her name.

52:01 A legendary professor's fraud case, and the school says it never heard of it
Stan Cohen was the first geneticist to move a gene from one living organism into another, and his 1970s recombinant DNA technique gave rise to the model of universities profiting from patents; in its final valid year that patent accounted for 62% of all Stanford patent revenue. In his freshman year, Theo found that Cohen had been found liable for fraud by a court: he had pitched investors on a drug target that might cure Huntington's disease, saying it was already approved to treat another condition, without telling them it had been permanently banned by the FDA in 1976 because it was lethal. He was ultimately ordered to pay $29 million and paid it. Theo asked the university, and the university replied that it had never heard of the case and had no involvement whatsoever — even though Stanford owned the relevant intellectual property and had been subpoenaed.

55:04 Raising money is easier than an internship, and that itself is the signal
The saying circulating in Stanford's inner circles is that raising money for a startup is easier than landing an internship — Theo says that's absurd, it shouldn't be that way, but that's the reality. He describes the moment as a game of AI musical chairs: everyone is waiting to see who is still standing when the music stops and who is left holding the bag. He isn't worried about cash-flow-positive companies like Meta and Google; he's worried about the companies clinging to the AI narrative that have no technology of their own, no revenue, and no ability to generate revenue — they can't hold on, and they will collapse. But he also cautions that Silicon Valley hasn't held power for long; it's a very immature power system that hasn't grown guardrails, transparency or accountability, and one collapse doesn't necessarily mean a reckoning.

item.title: America's Manufacturing Hollowing Out Isn't a Capability Problem, It's a Financial Return Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.description: Chris Power says America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement while China manages it like national security; tariffs are only an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing rivals' industrial capacity.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Power says America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement while China manages it like national security; tariffs are only an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing rivals' industrial capacity.

Two frontline hardware founders explain the real bottlenecks of American reindustrialization: not technology, but trust, cost, and how supply chains are defined. High information density; the second half on tariffs and subsidies is the most valuable.

2:02 The reserve currency is the first step of decline
Chris Power gives a four-step cycle: great powers first have a generative population and the best industrial capacity, then win or prevent a war, then become extremely lazy, and finally outsource the very things that made them successful. He says this cycle repeats roughly every 150 years: the Dutch gave way to the British, the British gave way to the Americans, and each time industrial power was re-traded for financial power, the world's reserve currency changed hands. This judgment was the starting point for his founding Hadrian: you think you're Mike Tyson at his peak, but your opponent thinks you're the Mike Tyson right before Buster Douglas knocked him out.

9:10 90% of the factory floor is a software problem
Chris Power says the biggest misconception about advanced manufacturing is that seeing people moving things around in a factory means it's a humanoid robot problem. In reality, 90% of advanced manufacturing is smart people sitting at computers doing digital engineering, or operating an extremely dumb computer on the shop floor. Welders or machinists have to stand in front of the machine because the system isn't closed-loop; they're doing trigonometry in their heads, judging whether the tool is about to snap. That's why Hadrian positions itself as a software company: it breaks physical tasks into high-judgment fixturing, then hands execution to robots, CNC, or welding systems.

14:14 Software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in LA
Tom Mueller says Southern California's aerospace talent ecosystem is recovering; three or four years after SpaceX was founded in 2002, the aerospace employment curve in the South Bay started trending up. He lists what this area is doing simultaneously: nuclear energy companies, drone companies, defense companies, 3D printing companies, plus Anduril in Orange County. The two companies poach from each other and compete for talent, and Northrop Grumman is right across the street from Impulse. Tom's summary: software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware is done in LA.

15:17 Vertical integration is for learning the problem, not saving money
Tom Mueller explains the real logic of SpaceX-style vertical integration: you have to build the first development engine or spacecraft yourself, because you need to learn all the assembly and machining problems during the prototype phase. If you hand it to a machine shop from the start, and the drawings have problems or the parts don't fit when they come back, you learn nothing. Once the design converges, then you outsource. Chris Power adds that every company should keep 10% to 15% of in-house capacity, because there's always a "hot pan" moment when you need a genius to make something within an hour to hit a flight milestone, but scale has to happen outside.

16:18 Outsourcing decisions are about trust, not finance
Chris Power says what's bought and sold in manufacturing is trust. Hadrian's vertical integration strategy is to outsource as much as possible to every reindustrialization startup and small business, because there are too many projects to run. But they will vertically integrate the links where they "don't believe you can deliver on time." This isn't a financial trade-off; they'd rather spend an extra two million dollars on equipment and hire a team than bet the risk on a traditional foundry that has been late on every submarine program for the past thirty years. His exact words: most of America is incompetent when it comes to trust and scheduling.

19:20 In World War II, America was China
Chris Power uses World War II as an analogy: German engineers crushed America on engineering, but America wore them down with McDonald's-style mass production and better logistics. He says America played the role in World War II that China plays today—not by having the best engineering, but by producing the most. Now the situation is reversed: American missile stockpiles run out in seven days in war games, and China built 2,600 ships while America built six. His conclusion: you can have the best Raytheon missiles, but if you can't mass-produce them, you have no options.

21:23 The robot bottleneck is the velocity of training data
Chris Power says the robot competition ultimately comes down to software, and software, especially AI, now comes down to the velocity of training data, which in turn depends on physical-world deployment—that is, mass manufacturing. So this isn't a friendly competition between American companies over "whether Tesla sells a few more Optimus units or Google wins"; it's a civilizational-level confrontation. Tom Mueller adds from the space angle: building on the Moon and Mars requires robot legions rather than humans, because the environment is too dangerous and too expensive; a good robot needs three things—dexterous hands, vision that's basically solved, and an AI brain.

29:40 Tariffs are an imperfect corrective tool
Chris Power says manufacturing has four inputs: energy, labor, cost of capital, and export tariffs. He has run the numbers: even if you set Hadrian's labor costs and energy costs to zero, importing components from China is still three times cheaper than buying raw materials in America and making them yourself. He argues China has run industrial policy like national security since 1985, subsidizing energy, labor, capital, and export tariffs, while America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement returns. The problem with tariffs is enforcement: ban only China and not Singapore, and Chinese companies route through Singapore; differences in the definition of raw materials and assembly also hurt American companies importing components from Mexico.

item.title: The Bat Doesn't Know What It's Like to Be a Bat Either
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.description: The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.
item.content:encoded:
The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.

The second half of episode 400, and listenable on its own. The first half is about theories of consciousness; the second half unexpectedly slides into animal ethics, and the four of them never do settle their disagreement.

1:07 A bat having an inner world is not the same as being conscious
Christopher summarises Dennett's response: he flatly denies Nagel — we can talk about what it's like to be a bat in all sorts of ways (by first ruling out the things bats don't do, for instance), and with enough information we eventually get there, because "what it's like to be a bat" just is the discriminative, dispositional states the bat has. Dylan supplies the step Dennett actually rejects: drawing on von Uexküll's Umwelt and Innenwelt (surrounding world and inner world), Dennett grants that the bat has an inner world, which is not crazy; what he won't accept is the inference straight from "has an inner world" to "therefore consciousness exists," and that is exactly the step Nagel uses to prove consciousness exists. Our mode of access is heterophenomenology: treat the bat's behaviour and physiology as a text in need of interpretation.

5:37 Consciousness is not an all-or-nothing property
Christopher reads out a passage from Dennett: are language-less animals not conscious at all? Dennett says the question shouldn't be taken as a matter of course, because it presupposes "something we've had a hard time getting rid of" — that consciousness is an all-or-nothing property, splitting the universe into two utterly different categories: things that have it and things that don't. That dichotomy is what Dennett wants to dismantle; what he wants is consciousness in degrees. Christopher then offers his own version: he doesn't want to accept property dualism, he wants to deny the hard problem, because subjectivity can perfectly well have a biological and evolutionary explanation — agency and subjectivity co-evolved; a physical process organised from the inside "feels like something," and that is a real biological phenomenon.

12:57 The bat doesn't know what it's like to be a bat either
Seth pushes the argument to its extreme: it isn't "we don't know what it's like to be a bat," it's that there is no "what it's like to be a bat as seen from the bat's side" at all; the bat doesn't know either, because it lacks the machinery to string experiences into a narrative and give them names. Dylan immediately marks out the cost of this inference: if anything with dynamic activity has its own experience, then atoms count too, and that's panpsychism. Christopher says you don't have to go as far as atoms, but concedes that the direction really does sound like panpsychism — he'd rather use a threshold: you need a feedback loop of sensing and acting before you can talk about a new way of being.

14:35 Even plants have a perspective in some sense
Mark digs up a line from Dennett's book: the perspective of a conscious observer is a refined descendant of the original perspective of the first replicators, which "divided the world into good and bad" — on that account even plants have a perspective in this sense, and "perspective" thereby becomes a metaphor. Christopher then offers gradualism: from sponges to mantis shrimp to humans, subjectivity accumulates layer by layer and gets thicker and thicker, with a fuzzy threshold in between. Dylan wants to nail the threshold down harder: you can't use "complex" as the criterion, since weather is a complex self-maintaining system too; the difference is that living things can replicate themselves and have a wholeness, so the only thing the Earth lacks is its own replication.

19:47 You are a bunch of things, not a soul
Mark finds Dennett's 1994 reply collection Get Real, which uses snakes as an example: a snake has no central representation of "mouse," it just responds to prey through three separate sensory systems. Dennett's point is that the perceptual system we take to be a single whole is really a pile of little homunculi each making its own discriminations; you are not an Aristotelian form, a soul, an organisation that runs you — we are all a bunch of things. Christopher objects: failure to integrate information processing doesn't mean there's no self — the two hemispheres of a split-brain patient are also separate, and we don't conclude from that that he has no self; the snake may still have a more ancient, minimal sense of boundary and evaluative experience.

27:39 Reducing experience to discrimination looks a lot like behaviourism
Christopher says he agrees with Dennett 99%, and is stuck on the 1%: when Dennett wants to reduce a person to dispositional states, saying that experiencing red is nothing over and above being able to discriminate red from non-red and being in that discriminative state, it sounds like behaviourism. Seth offers a defence: even if the substrate is just discriminative states, subjective experience, the self, is a composite stitched together out of memory, imagination, representation and symbolic language — it weaves scattered discriminative states into a story with descriptions, meanings and colour, and that story is me. Christopher agrees about the narrative self, but points out that the bat lacks the metacognitive capacity to construct such a self.

38:54 You can club an iguana, but not a rabbit
Mark says "everyone is a world" is a good moral fiction, but he doesn't know how to apply it to animals: there are too many iguanas in Florida, and encouraging everyone to go out and club them, he says, is completely fine and humane; swap in a rabbit and he won't accept it. Seth offers an evolutionary explanation: our feelings about animals domesticated over tens of thousands of years, wild animals and reptiles were never the same to begin with, and this doesn't conflict with "the self is a narrative centre of gravity." Christopher anchors it in valence: animals are not reflex machines, they are situated perspectives that evaluate, and that is the reason they enter moral consideration — he says that after reading Lars Chittka's The Mind of a Bee, his own way of dealing with bees changed.

46:10 Take away caring and nothing of the pain is left
Mark turns to where Dennett talks specifically about pain: what is the functional relation of pain? If you take away caring about it and wanting to avoid it, take away everything else, and leave only the sensation of pain, then nothing is left — your not liking the pain is itself part of the pain. Mark says this is exactly Dennett's attitude to philosophical zombies: imagine someone biologically, behaviourally, even in their internal relations exactly like you, but the light of consciousness never came on — Dennett thinks this is so absurd that it's hard even to explain to scientists.

item.title: Beijing's Central Axis Is Not a Relic — It's a City Operating System Still Running
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-historyhit-北京中轴线不是古迹-是仍在运转的城市操作系统/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-historyhit-北京中轴线不是古迹-是仍在运转的城市操作系统/
item.description: The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier in the Kaogong Ji, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.
item.content:encoded:
The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier in the Kaogong Ji, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.

Medium information density, but its strength is restoring the central axis from tourist attraction to a planning logic still in force — suited to anyone interested in cities and organisational design.

7:13 A two-thousand-year-old instruction manual is still in use
When the Ming set out to rebuild the capital, they dug up a technical manual more than two thousand years old, the Kaogong Ji (“考工记”). It specified a city four to five kilometres on each side, three gates per side, the palace at the centre, an ancestral temple on one side, the court in front, the market behind, and a Temple of Heaven in the southern suburbs. The historian Jeremiah Jenik says the logic behind this layout was cosmic order: there is a fixed point in the sky, the North Star, so there should be a corresponding fixed point on earth, and the most fitting fixed point is the emperor himself — placing yourself in the palace at the exact centre of the city is placing yourself inside a cosmic order that revolves around you.

9:16 They actually built it to the drawing
The most astonishing thing is not that the Ming dared to use a blueprint over a thousand years old, but how closely they built to it. Overlay the Kaogong Ji drawing on the model at the Beijing Planning Exhibition Hall and the two almost coincide. So Beijing today is still a twenty-first-century city running around a fifteenth-century heart, and that heart follows principles laid down nearly two thousand years ago. Compare London, which grew organically along the Thames: Beijing had the blueprint first, the city second.

11:20 The central axis is a spine, and the city grew out of it
From north to south, the axis strings together the Bird's Nest, the Drum and Bell Towers, Jingshan, the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, and finally Yongdingmen at the southern end. The show likens it to a spine: everything is planned and expanded outward from this line. Running true north-south and aligned with the heavens, the line has been Beijing's most distinctive feature for six hundred years, and it determines the shape of the city today.

12:22 The right to tell time is the right to rule
The Drum and Bell Towers were the timekeeping centre of the whole city, and the bell was said to carry twenty kilometres. From 1272 all the way to 1924 — the year the last Qing emperor left the Forbidden City — the time struck here was Beijing's official time. The drum was beaten one hundred and eight times every two hours; it was the first sound Beijingers heard in the morning and the last they heard at night. The show says it is almost as if the emperor were not merely marking time but claiming ownership of time itself.

15:32 Jingshan was piled up out of the previous dynasty's rubble
Jingshan is not a natural hill; it was built artificially by the Yongle Emperor according to feng shui principles. An ideal palace faces south, with water to the south — water that should curve and flow to bring qi and life — and a mountain to the north to block the evil qi coming from that direction and display authority. Beijing is too far from the Yan Mountains to the north, so the Ming took the rubble of the old Mongol palaces and the earth dug out of new canals and built a symbolic mountain inside the city.

18:52 The Forbidden City was a super-project of nationwide mobilisation
Ten thousand logs were shipped from 1,800 kilometres to the southwest, the golden bricks of Suzhou came from 1,100 kilometres to the south — 18 million bricks fired in all — and gold leaf came from Nanjing. One million labourers plus more than 100,000 craftsmen built it in fifteen years. From the 1420s to the early twentieth century, twenty-four emperors lived here. Today it receives more than 15 million visitors a year, making it the most visited historic site on earth.

22:55 A nail-free timber structure can take a magnitude 9.5 quake
These buildings are almost entirely wood, and what lets them stand for centuries is the dougong (斗拱): the dou are the bearing blocks, the gong are inserted and interlock very tightly. Wood shrinks and warps, and this system lets it deform flexibly while keeping the overall structure intact; in an earthquake every small piece of wood can slide a little, rather than shearing the bearing blocks or popping the bolts. Scientists have calculated that this construction could withstand the strongest earthquake ever recorded, magnitude 9.5.

23:57 It was struck by lightning within a year of completion
The Forbidden City was not fireproof. Less than a year after it was completed in 1421, the three great halls were burned to ashes by lightning. Afterwards 308 bronze vats were installed to store water against the next fire. The detail makes the point: no matter how precise the planning, it cannot stop a single point of failure — you can only add redundancy after the fact.

item.title: Germany's CDU Falls Out of a State Parliament: The Era of the Centre Is Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.description: The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right command an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.
item.content:encoded:
The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right command an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.

This is a piece of German domestic political commentary, not an interview. Information density is moderate, but it lays out the judgment that "populism has become the mainstream" very clearly — suited to anyone watching the direction of European politics.

0:00 The CDU is shut out of a state parliament for the first time
In the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state election, the CDU won under 5% of the vote and therefore holds no seats in that state parliament — the first time this has happened in the history of the Federal Republic. In the same election the AfD took roughly 38% of the vote, once again becoming the state's largest party. The author calls this Merz's "final nail in the coffin": he may hold on as chancellor for a few more weeks or months, but his authority has vanished, his capacity to shape the country is completely exhausted — in political language, "a dead man walking."

0:00 The CDU's decline came later than the SPD's but is just as fatal
The CDU is the most important party in postwar German history, governing the Federal Republic for 53 of the past 77 years, and from Adenauer to Kohl to Merkel it left its mark on every aspect of the country. The author points out that in the early 2000s everyone was talking about "the crisis of social democracy," with the SPD falling from over 40% support to record lows; in hindsight, the fate of the centre-left big party was merely a leading indicator of a broader crisis of the entire political centre, and the CDU subsequently walked the same road. The era of what Germans call the Volksparteien — catch-all parties capable of mobilising most of the vote — is effectively over.

0:00 Populists are not a fringe phenomenon but the most important political force
The author says this has been the most-asked question of the past decade: "Will the populist wave continue, or is it about to peak?" When Trump became the Republican nominee in the summer of 2016 and Britain voted for Brexit, the answer seemed obvious to him; now the answer is undeniable — the populists are here to stay. What looked abnormal a few years ago has, whether you like it or not, become the mainstream. Populist politicians now hold power in the United States, India, Turkey and many parts of the democratic world, and there is a high probability they will take power in France and Brazil in the coming months. Even where they remain in opposition, they are already strong enough to destroy any sense of business as usual.

0:00 The rise of one extremist party is feeding another
In the Berlin state election, Die Linke took 26% of the vote and emerged the big winner. The party descends from the SED, which ruled East Germany with an iron fist, and after reunification initially appealed mainly to older voters nostalgic for the security of the communist system; in recent years it has reinvented itself in the image of the global illiberal left, which the author considers roughly comparable to Zack Polanski's Greens in Britain or the more extreme parts of the DSA in the United States. During the campaign, some of the party's supporters were filmed chanting "Yalla, Yalla Intifada!"; on election night, the head of a notorious crime family visited the party's election party and cheerfully told the media he felt an affinity with it. The party's leader will very likely now become the next mayor of Berlin — the first time an heir to the SED takes power in the capital.

0:00 Voters under 35 have swung to the two extremes
Another notable feature of the two elections is the age distribution. The SPD and CDU, which once dominated Germany's political landscape, draw most of their support from pensioners. Among voters under 35, Die Linke and the AfD hold unassailable majorities in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. From this the author concludes that the coming years will bring an even larger tilt toward the extremes. This also explains why the collapse of the centre is not a one-off election accident: the structure of the electorate itself is pushing the scales toward the two ends.

0:00 Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's left coalition is just an election accident
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, because a batch of other parties all failed to clear the 5% threshold for entering parliament, a broad left coalition just barely won enough votes to govern. But the author stresses this is an election accident unlikely to be repeated — a gap of a few thousand votes would leave the state completely ungovernable. The point is crucial: when centrist parties fall below the threshold, they don't just lose their own seats, they push the governability of the entire state to the edge of a cliff.

0:00 Don't surrender, and don't deny the problem is real
The author explicitly rejects two reactions. The first is to urge the centre to surrender: if the political centre can't hold, moderates might as well defect to the extremists on "their own side." He thinks this is wrong — neither Die Linke nor the AfD can solve the real problems Germany faces, and despite their enormous differences the two have conspicuous similarities, from their ambiguity toward Moscow to their persistent inability to purge antisemites from their ranks. The second is to keep denying reality: for a decade the centre has attributed the extremists' success to foreign interference, social media algorithms, some candidate's tactical blunder, or the stupidity, sexism or racism of voters. The author says these ways of blinding yourself to the facts in front of you may be comforting, but they are equally dangerous.

item.title: Going global: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and the US — go there first so you can get big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.description: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and the US once they're big, but it's exactly backwards — you go there so you can get big. Pick the wrong region and nothing that follows — product 3.0, the channel pyramid — can be built.
item.content:encoded:
Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and the US once they're big, but it's exactly backwards — you go there so you can get big. Pick the wrong region and nothing that follows — product 3.0, the channel pyramid — can be built.

Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas-investing experience into four choices, counterintuitive but each backed by cases and numbers; the back half, on AI rebuilding organisations and pricing, has the highest information density.

1:30 The old cross-border mega-seller playbook is dead
Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-style mindset, running dozens or hundreds of accounts; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. Ten years ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and plenty of investors loved them. But a distribution-style company is essentially a traffic-style company: the more stores, the more likely you are to get traffic. When a platform's goods aren't plentiful enough, he doesn't oppose distribution; once goods are plentiful enough, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, there are three red lines: goods not matching the listing harms consumers, brushing orders harms other merchants, and slipping in little cards to build private traffic harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel cares deeply about consumer experience, and these behaviours run straight into that protective wall.

4:38 Of the four choices, region comes first
Wei Zhe says it's not just cross-border e-commerce — all of life is about choice mattering more than effort. He gives four choices: region, channel, product category, brand positioning. On region he has always argued for seizing the European and US markets first, because paying power is strong, internet penetration is high, and more importantly a brand can build momentum there. This isn't something they invented: when Japanese and Korean brands went global back then, they all seized Europe and the US. On category, they change their advice every three years: the first three years they backed products common to China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification — like Anker's power banks, which back then were almost identical apart from the voltage; the second three years they advised overseas-exclusive products, because China's supply chain had all gone overseas and China-abroad commonality offered no differentiation; the last three years it's product 3.0 — powered, chipped, algorithmic.

12:29 It's not that you go to Europe and the US once you're big — you go there to get big
Many companies tell Wei Zhe ‘I'll go to Europe and the US when I'm big’; he says it's exactly backwards — you go to Europe and the US so you can get big. He cites the swimwear company Cupshe: a husband and wife, 50,000 dollars of inventory, and the first stop was the US. 50,000 dollars is sales inventory, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. Looking recently at AI smart hardware, they start from a thousand or ten thousand products on the Kickstarter crowdfunding platform, even taking prepayment before placing orders, with no capital — that's also a great way to test the water. He even advises big companies entering the European and US markets to learn from small startups. They always say the needle must be fine enough to pierce through; big and small companies alike should first nail the four singles: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

20:36 After AI, good companies don't just find demand — they create it
Wei Zhe says that with AI, excellent companies shouldn't go looking for demand; they should lead demand and create demand. He cites a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: originally unpowered, they electrified it, added a chip and an algorithm — the algorithm is actually very simple, with GPS positioning, since the map of the sky's movements is regular. He wasn't an astronomy hobbyist before but would buy one: at home in Silicon Valley you tap once, it automatically aligns Orion for you, tells you three in the morning is the best time, you set it and go to sleep, and the next day it has taken the shots for you. This lets anyone become a very good astronomy hobbyist. Another example: a cross-border class student doing curtains, which didn't sell well in the US after being powered, because American electricians are expensive; so he put a solar panel on the window, turning electric curtains that need an electrician into something you can DIY. Revenue went from one or two hundred million to four or five hundred million, and profit is now one or two hundred million.

24:48 In the AI era, still charging subscriptions means you're behind
Wei Zhe says that in the AI era, still thinking in terms of subscription fees means you're behind again; they're all urging companies toward back-end charging, software charging — tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest approach, a bit like advertising that used to charge by time rather than by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks off this month, isn't subscribing for the month a waste of two weeks? They advise that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not go back to the old SaaS model of 9.99 dollars a month. One AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and charges nothing if you don't read; the same for smart bike trainers — after topping up, one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

27:28 Adding AI is more worth backing than AI adding
Wei Zhe has a view he calls AI-plus versus plus-AI; he flips the phrase around and says he's more bullish on plus-AI than on today's AI-plus. The difference: plus-AI is hardware humans have already accepted, which you AI-ify; rather than using AI to create hardware never seen before. It's very hard for humans to accept an entirely new piece of hardware. Take Oura making a ring, because you accepted rings first; something that hangs a camera under your neck is harder for me — I've never accepted that hardware. So they're very bullish on adding AI to already-accepted hardware. One capacitive stylus they invested in is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad; it doesn't add an extra pen for you, it just AI-ifies that pen. He also particularly wants to transform one of the top one or two overseas fitness-equipment companies, replacing the fitness coach on the screen with an AI-generated one — you want a man, it's a man; you want a Black coach, it's a Black coach; install two cameras and it can coach your workout with AI.

29:43 Channels aren't laid out flat — they're a pyramid
Wei Zhe says channels aren't about more channels meaning more roads, with each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and rules about which channel a new product launches in first. What counts as a light-goods channel, what counts as the main waist channel for volume — the pyramid design differs by category and brand. He cites Anker: making power banks and mecha gear seems a bit low, so to enter the consumer-electronics high ground of Soundcore headphones it had to get into Apple flagship stores; whether it really sells a lot doesn't matter, but it can transform the brand — Apple is the pinnacle of the pyramid. Pop Mart must open on London's Oxford Street; even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose — but it must hold that position. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels for selling goods, which definitely won't work: AliExpress is a light-goods channel, somewhere to dump stock after Amazon delists you; you can't sell on Amazon and here too, and consumers get confused.

36:14 R&D is the 1, marketing is the 0
Wei Zhe says he really dislikes splashing out on marketing spend. Many Chinese brands going overseas or cross-border e-commerce are happy to add 2% of revenue to marketing spend, but consumers don't get it. He says: do you dare add 2% of revenue to R&D spend? He has met many bosses at the one or two billion scale; at one billion they say 20 million for R&D, and I don't know what for. He says, see, there's the problem — you don't know what for. Your 2% thrown at marketing spend makes the platform happy and consumers get nothing; but 2% thrown into R&D, consumers get it. He has always firmly believed a good product speaks for itself, and marketing is just — your R&D is the 1, marketing is the 0; if your thing is good you can amplify it, but if you don't have that 1, absolutely don't put on a lot of 0s. He gives three signals for judging: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and crush it by doubling its performance; second, you sell at the same price as it; third, you sell online and hit a point where offline channels come looking for you.

item.title: The AI office hype hasn't cleared, and the personal Agent war has already begun | Breaking down Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse
