item.description: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.
item.content:encoded:
Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.

Four frontline product people break down four routes — Town, Instinct, Grok Bot, Muse — and also explain why that batch of products like Xiaolongxia became martyrs. Information density is high, but the second half is worth more.

0:00 100,000 users prop up a $10 billion valuation
Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still hadn't reached 100,000 users, yet its valuation rose from $50 million at the start of the year to $500 million in August, then $2.5 billion at the end of August, and this month the market is circulating a new round priced at $10 billion, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old unknown with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan put it bluntly: what capital is buying is neither the founder nor the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI, and it can pay the price of the next-generation personal operating system to grab a ticket.

15:16 The line between tool and person is proactivity
The biggest difference between this wave of Agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. Two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs the context explained again every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are like a friend or colleague; second, proactivity — in Manus, setting up an automated task still depends on prompts, on you spelling out the rules and intent, and that isn't proactivity. True proactivity is subjective initiative — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and comes over on their own to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

18:09 Office Agents organise by project, personal Agents organise by person
The core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along the dimension of a mission or project, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centred on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside you are AI companions you can drive together. In personal scenarios people care less about model capability and the harness layer, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks; office Agents are the ones that really care about task completion rates.

30:28 Town starts by trading email for the user's mandate
The four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile app, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC; it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you send and receive often, auto-archives, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends automatically after you tap confirm. It goes deeper in the email scenario than any other agent, and overseas it has already achieved fairly viral spread, especially in school-related scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and acquire the user's ultimate mandate bit by bit.

39:33 Poke didn't break out, and it wasn't a technical limit
Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make a standalone app, but Poke didn't break out. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limit — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could absolutely have done it at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-mandate route, able to access credit cards, screen and microphone, booking flights and buying things for you — things users hadn't seen before, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content push accuracy, taking the proactive push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it didn't take the step of "finishing the thing for you".

42:39 A cloud Agent has to handle three environments
Mark says doing a cloud agent was a painful lesson: a local agent and a cloud agent are completely different things. To do personal AI you have to be usable anytime, anywhere — you can't be unreachable just because the computer screen is off. The cloud has to handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context passing between the three are very complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably on the cloud took at least two months; setting aside detours, polishing a sincere piece of work takes at least three to four months.

50:39 Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two businesses
Town started out doing corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios; the relationship is more like you paying to hire a personal assistant, which naturally filters for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and short on time and energy. Muse is more like a middleman, a shopping guide, a broker — although it has a paid subscription, the main projected revenue source is still commission from matchmaking transactions, aimed at mass users, blending into everyday WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, and the scenarios they cut into and the users they filter out are different too.

1:14:07 For an Agent, your saved folder may be noise
The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was: extract what you like to eat from ingredients saved on Instagram, generate a shopping list, adjust the menu by dinner party size and dietary restrictions, then complete the shopping and relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, going from a discovery platform to a decision-and-transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is to save face for the free business narrative: helping users close transactions is absolutely not among the top scenarios users want solved; users more want to solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in saved folders; the truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram saves may themselves be noise to an agent.

item.title: Ten Years of Parenting Taught Me: When Your Kid Won't Listen, the Problem Isn't Your Kid
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.description: On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as truth — each one first learned in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.
item.content:encoded:
On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as truth — each one first learned in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.

For parents who want to interrogate their own parenting methodology. Medium information density, heavy on personal narrative, but the ten reflections are clearly structured, and the back half — on the ‘village’ and on the couple relationship — is more valuable than the front half.

6:00 Forcing the medicine won the behavior and lost the relationship
The host recalls her three-year-old daughter refusing antibiotics; she held her down and forced the medicine in, and her daughter threw most of it back up. That night her husband Alvin spent an hour with their daughter in the bathroom, calmly saying the whole time, ‘I'm willing to do anything, but we're not leaving until we figure this out.’ In the end the daughter finished the whole course herself, with small sips of medicine, small sips of water, and a small piece of chocolate to take the taste away. The host says the difference wasn't that her husband was more patient — it's that he wasn't solving a behavior, he was understanding what would actually help the child do this thing. What the child needed was autonomy over the process, and to feel she was on the same team as her parent rather than being held down to do something.

9:19 The authoritative parenting framework rests on 146 white kids
The host says she accepted uncritically early on that ‘authoritative is the best parenting style,’ because every blog and every study said so. It wasn't until she did the episode on corporal punishment that she found a paper co-authored by Diana Baumrind defending parents' ability to spank their children, and started digging. She found that this framework — cited more than 26,000 times, and defining sixty years of parenting research — was originally based on just 146 white, middle-class preschoolers in the town where Baumrind lived. She calls this evidence of her own insufficient critical thinking, and says she now asks at the macro level ‘does this theory make sense,’ and at the micro level ‘does it fit this specific child in front of me.’

17:41 Not punishing your kid doesn't mean being ruled by your kid
The host says she once believed that without punishment and consequences children would run wild — she even stood in the shower when her daughter was four months old thinking ‘how do I discipline her without becoming a mean mom.’ Clinical psychologist Dr. Houri Parsi admitted in the membership community that she too had treated ‘obedience’ as the goal, and that every tooth-brushing was a battle. Once, recording for the host to see, she deliberately used no threats, no punishments, no rewards, and simply asked her two-year-old son ‘why don't you want to brush your teeth.’ He couldn't put it into words — he just called out ‘Mama’ and buried his head in her chest. She realized what he wanted was time alone with her. She put the toilet lid down, sat down, held her son, and they sang a song together — and he brushed his own teeth, the whole thing in under five minutes.

21:31 ‘I need you to take out the trash’ is not a need
The host says that looking back, she didn't understand what a ‘need’ was — she thought saying ‘I need you to take out the trash’ to her husband was a perfectly logical sentence. Before their daughter was born the two of them almost never argued: mountain biking in summer, skiing in winter, because the ad agency they worked at represented resorts and paid them in vouchers. After their daughter was born everything changed: during his three weeks of paternity leave her husband would fetch her anything she wanted, and the rest of the time he was training for a hundred-mile ride and watching the Tour de France. She says it was learning that she had needs for ‘collaboration, partnership, having my effort seen’ that actually pried open the problems between them; before that she was carrying a large amount of resentment inside her with no idea how to handle it.

24:01 When you're triggered, the problem isn't the person who interrupted you
The host says her biggest trigger is being interrupted — the moment her husband interrupts her she flies into a rage, most recently over how much postage a package needed. She always assumed the cause was simply that her husband interrupted her, and that if he stopped, everything would be fine. In July 2018, recording with intergenerational trauma expert Dr. Rebecca Babcock-Fenerci, she traced it live to her own father, a special education teacher who treated sixteen-year-olds like ten-year-olds and for a stretch lectured her every night. Later, in the car, she interrupted her daughter, and her daughter said ‘Don't interrupt me, Mama,’ and her husband looked at her and said ‘She is you.’ She says that was the moment she realized it had never been only about the two people in the room, and out of it she developed the ‘Tame Your Triggers’ course, which grew from a one-month module to ten weeks.

30:27 The handmade book she made while pregnant was full of expectations for her child
The host describes a book she made while pregnant: three covers, one in the middle and one on each side, opening in both directions, brown book cloth with a beige spine, the word ‘me’ cut out of the board on one cover and ‘you’ embossed on the other when you flipped it over — the concept being ‘you came out of me.’ On the ‘me’ side she wrote her own feelings and thoughts; on the ‘you’ side she wrote to the not-yet-met Carys. She reads out the earliest batch of ‘expectations for you’: I hope you're smart, or at least average; I hope you're the kind of child who shakes hands with people instead of hiding behind my legs; I hope you like roughhousing and also like pretty things; I hope you don't cry all the time; I hope when you fall you pick yourself up and say ‘I'm okay.’ She says looking back, the biggest mistake was not knowing how to simply be with a person, to let them be their whole self and witness it, without carrying ideas about how they should be.

33:14 Kohn's principle two: reconsider your demands first
The host says she once thought she'd play the role of ‘enforcer’ — she even wrote ‘I hope you can love me as much as he does’ on her pregnancy expectations list. She says RIE loosened the soil for her, but what actually planted the seed was Alfie Kohn's Unconditional Parenting. She shares a few of its principles: principle two is to reconsider your demands — ‘maybe when a child won't do what you ask, the problem isn't the child, it's what you're asking’; principle five is to change the way you see, not just the way you act — when you see your child do the thing you asked them not to do, your first reaction is curiosity about what they're struggling with, not how to make them stop; principle ten is ‘attribute to your child the best motive consistent with the observed facts,’ and she says when she quotes it she changes the ending to ‘consistent with the observed behavior,’ because ‘there are no facts, only what we observe.’

39:07 The couple relationship isn't a different subject, it's the same one
The host says she long believed the couple relationship and the parent-child relationship were completely different things — when she started the parenting membership eight years ago she asked Dr. Laura Froyen to write the co-parenting module, because she had no idea how to handle a partner relationship. She says her parenting shift toward collaboration was relatively easy, because she had no ten-year-old habits with her daughter; but with Alvin she'd been together ten years without ever learning how to disagree, because most of that time was spent doing hobbies they loved, and she didn't mind doing most of the housework. It wasn't until she took Gottman training that she realized this was almost the same work she'd been doing with her child all these years — while also believing the Gottman method itself has a few key flaws. She recruited couples from the membership to record real arguments, using modified tools, and one couple whose husband had refused to discuss a toxic issue was willing to talk after his wife listened for ten minutes with a genuine intent to understand him — and in that same session they reached an agreement to move forward.

item.title: NPR's comment section was flagged as bots. It was actually a group of middle schoolers.
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.description: NPR staff saw gibberish flooding a comment section and reported it as bots; a younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.
item.content:encoded:
NPR staff saw gibberish flooding a comment section and reported it as bots; a younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.

Four independent stories, medium information density, but the generational misread in the first story and the mother-daughter conversation about braiding in the third are both worth hearing.

1:01 The gibberish comments weren't bots, they were kids
Dave Blanchard saw a sudden flood of incomprehensible comments on the Wild Card comment section on Spotify, assumed bots, and reported them to Spotify and had them deleted. But Hannah Chin, a colleague at NPR ten years younger, opened the screenshots and immediately reached the opposite conclusion: these are kids. Her evidence was the display names with emoji you need a special character generator to type, the cartoon avatars she'd never seen, and the back-and-forth short sentences with piles of exclamation points. Dave didn't buy it at first, replying, "That's an interesting theory."

6:05 Using playlists as a group-chat entrance
Hannah kept digging and found how the kids operated: one kid creates a public playlist called Let's Chat Here or New Chat with just one podcast episode in it; other kids see the playlist, click into that episode, and chat in the comments. They also posted Google Forms as quizzes, writing "only cool people can fill this out." Hannah said bots don't go post Google Forms, but Gen Alpha does, the way her own generation made UQuiz or BuzzFeed personality quizzes. That was the point where Dave was convinced.

8:06 They picked NPR because the comment section was empty
The show contacted several commenters, and only one, a 14-year-old girl named Ella, agreed to be interviewed; she did it from the car while her father drove. Ella said the core group is about 20 kids, many in drama club, mostly girls, with strict parents who don't let them use regular social media. They first chatted in the comment section of a podcast that played TikTok videos; after that podcast got shut down, the kids started moving from playlist to playlist. Asked why they chose NPR shows, Ella said: we look for podcasts that don't have many comments, so we don't get mixed up in other people's comments.

11:08 Dave needed a generational translator
After learning the truth, Dave said he felt guilty for reporting them, and also felt old. He said, "I literally needed Hannah to be my generational translator," and that this made him acutely aware of his age and how out of date he was. Ella said she's sure that one day she too will be as completely baffled as Dave. The show puts this segment at the top, as the entry point to the episode's "Intergenerational Space Travel" theme.

25:35 The wedding toast was a poem nobody understood
At 18, Courtney read a poem she wrote at her mother's second wedding, and her mother held it against her for thirty years. The poem opens with the mother walking in habitual darkness, every breath like her last; the middle has the mother standing by the counter smoking; the ending turns to "you found roots, you found a soul worth worshipping." The mother said that on the wedding day she only heard the negative first half and never heard the kindness at the end; rereading it, Courtney admitted that presenting a bride with such a dark picture on her wedding day really would make it impossible to hear the good part.

31:52 The body knew the marriage was wrong first
Two days after the wedding, the 49-year-old mother suffered a massive stroke. Courtney offers a theory: the mother's body, not her mind, had known all along that the marriage was a mistake. The mother agreed, saying she knew when she bought the wedding dress, that she wasn't that happy then, that she "anticipated this awfulness ahead of time," sensing it in every fiber. This exchange turns all the earlier argument about the wedding toast into a question about why her mother didn't listen to her intuition back then.

39:05 Only kicking out the stepfather repaired mother and daughter
Last October, the mother fell in the kitchen Mr. X designed and broke her back; Mr. X was too drunk to help and only handed her the phone hours later so she could call an ambulance herself. The mother was hospitalized for months and gave Courtney power of attorney to go to court and get Mr. X out. Courtney said it was the hardest thing she's ever done, but they won. The mother said it was precisely because Courtney spent so much time here for that that she realized how much her daughter cared about her. Mr. X drove them apart, and kicking him out pulled them back together.

55:41 The mother says braiding shouldn't be an entry point to toughness
Myra Flynn locked horns with her six-year-old daughter Avalon every morning over braiding, and blurted out "sometimes what we need isn't comfortable," then realized those were her own mother's words. She called her mother, Martha Mathis, expecting support, but her mother said: braiding shouldn't be used as an entry point to make a child tough, because it carries too many racial and gender meanings; and six-year-old Avalon is already the toughest little girl there is. Her mother's advice was to let Avalon handle a small section of hair herself, because "she'll be gentle with herself."

item.title: The woman who killed Marat, and why the court wouldn't believe she acted alone
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-restishistory-刺杀马拉的女人-为什么法庭不信她独自行动/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-restishistory-刺杀马拉的女人-为什么法庭不信她独自行动/
item.description: Corday had her declaration written before the assassination and insisted after her arrest that she acted alone, yet the Revolutionary Tribunal kept pressing her on the "chain of conspiracy" — they could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a monster.
item.content:encoded:
Corday had her declaration written before the assassination and insisted after her arrest that she acted alone, yet the Revolutionary Tribunal kept pressing her on the "chain of conspiracy" — they could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a monster.

High information density: it links the institutional origins of the Terror, paper-money inflation and the Vendée war into a single causal chain, and the second half's assassination detail is especially valuable.

0:00 The assassination declaration was written before the act
When Corday was arrested she was carrying a declaration titled "To the Friends of Law and Peace in France." In it she named Marat "the most vile of villains," said he "has been condemned by the universe, and is therefore outside the law," and called on the French to "rise. Strike. Strike." This text was not a post-hoc defence — it was written before the act. What she wanted was not escape, but to turn her own death into a rallying point.

9:30 Marat was the first modern populist
Keith Michael Baker's new biography positions Marat as the first modern populist. His formula included: constantly invoking the capitalized "People," and claiming the people were at every moment in danger of being betrayed by appeasers and traitors; an obsession with conspiracy theory, stating outright that his goal was to keep his readers "perpetually on their guard," lest they be dragged into the abyss by royalists, priests and their ilk. The show points out that this "wake up, sheep" language is used today by both left and right.

21:57 Paper-money inflation pushed the poor into the streets
In early 1793 France had suffered years of poor harvests, the national grain market had collapsed, and the government had no money to fight its wars, so it printed paper money — the assignat — with roughly four billion in circulation. This triggered severe inflation, the price of bread and sugar soared, there were protests in the market almost daily, and women's marches appeared in the streets of Paris. The show stresses: these were the very same conditions that had set off the Revolution and the storming of the Bastille, and the poor would think, "the Revolution happened, yet life hasn't improved — so someone must be scheming."

32:13 The commander-in-chief's defection confirmed the conspiracy theories
On 8 March 1793 the Austrians counter-attacked and routed Dumouriez at Neerwinden; he was forced to withdraw from Belgium and Holland. He wanted to emulate Sulla and march on Paris as a military dictator, and asked his troops, "Shall we march on Paris?" They answered no. On 5 April he rode over to the Austrian lines, taking a number of senior officers with him, including the future King of France, Louis Philippe. One volunteer wrote to his mother: "Who can we trust now?"

38:27 The Terror machine was improvised, not designed
The show stresses that the key institutions of the Terror had no blueprint and no plan — they were built as they went along, and only in hindsight assembled into a machine, and many of those who helped build it were eventually swallowed by it. On 10 March the Revolutionary Tribunal was established to try political crimes, with death sentences to be carried out within 24 hours and no right of appeal; it sat in the Palais de Justice in Paris, and its cellars were the existing Conciergerie prison. Danton said: "Let us be terrible, so that the people need not be."

42:37 The Girondins used a new rule to strike at Marat, and it backfired
The Girondins had just abolished parliamentary immunity, and while large numbers of deputies were away on missions to the provinces, they indicted Marat on 14 April, accusing him of inciting insurrection. Marat went into hiding for three days, then, seeing that street opinion in Paris was on his side, turned himself in for trial. On 24 April the court convened in the Palais de Justice; the prosecutor, Fuquietanville, was a Montagnard sympathizer and let Marat deliver a long self-defence. The ten-man jury acquitted him within a few hours, and Marat was carried back to the National Convention by some 800 people, crowned with roses, to cries of "vive la république, vive Marat." For the Girondins it was a total humiliation.

1:04:31 Corday buys a knife: a 15-centimetre kitchen knife with a black handle
At around eight in the morning on 13 July, Charlotte Corday left her hotel, walked to the arcades of the Palais-Royal, bought a newspaper (which said the Convention would likely sentence the imprisoned Girondin deputies to death), and bought a black Paris hat with a green ribbon, replacing the white Norman-style cap that marked her out. She went into a cutler's shop called Le Coutelier Badin and bought a kitchen knife with a black handle and a blade about 15 centimetres long. Between 11:30 a.m. and noon she took a carriage to Marat's home on the rue des Cordeliers, but she had no appointment and was turned away by Marat's sister-in-law.

1:10:51 The court would not believe a woman could act alone
Corday was arrested on the spot, and one of her interrogators was Jean-Baptiste Drouet, the postmaster who had recognized Louis XVI's flight at Varennes. From the outset she said she had acted alone. But the Revolutionary Tribunal repeatedly interrogated her about the "chain of conspiracy," convinced she must be part of a Girondin plot. The interrogator Montané said: it is impossible, because you say Marat was the source of all France's ills, yet Marat was precisely the man who never stopped exposing traitors and conspirators, so someone must have lied to you. Corday replied: you are mad — only in Paris do people see Marat; in the other provinces he is taken for a monster. The court could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a bad man.

item.title: Intel's Optane Died Because 3D NAND Was Too Cheap, Not Because the Tech Was Bad
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.description: Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it got squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.
item.content:encoded:
Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it got squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.

A complete history of a failed memory technology, from RMM in 1970 to the Optane shutdown in 2022. Medium information density; the back half on data-center deployment and Micron's exit is the most valuable part.

3:07 The physics of phase-change memory is what makes it slow
Phase-change memory stores data by switching a material between a crystalline and an amorphous state: the crystalline state has low resistance, the amorphous state high resistance, and the two differ by three to four orders of magnitude. Melting the material and quenching it into the amorphous state is called RESET; the reverse is called SET. SET either melts the material into a liquid and lets it cool slowly into a crystal, or heats it to a temperature high enough to convert it directly to crystalline without melting. The author points out that SET is often the speed bottleneck for PCM. This physical mechanism has not changed since Stanford Ovshinsky discovered the phase-change behavior of chalcogenide compounds in the 1960s.

4:13 Intel built phase-change memory in 1970, then forgot about it
In 1970, RG Neale and DL Nelson of Energy Conversion Devices and Intel's Gordon Moore published an article in Electronics magazine announcing "Read-Mostly Memory," positioned between RAM and ROM, for storing data that programs read often but rarely change. Each cell was a silicon diode plus a layer of phase-change material; Intel supplied the silicon substrate, ECD supplied the material. But in 1970 the minimum feature size was only 10 microns, power consumption was high, SET took milliseconds, and endurance was low. DRAM capacity was growing, EPROM arrived, and RMM disappeared. Years later someone asked the 79-year-old Moore about the article, and he said he had no memory of it at all.

9:25 Numonyx treated PCM as its only shot at a comeback
The rise of NAND sent NOR flash into a long decline, and in 2007 global NOR sales fell 9% year over year. Intel merged its NOR business with STMicroelectronics' flash business, forming the Swiss company Numonyx in 2008, with an investment from Francisco Partners and bank loans. NOR had none of NAND's growth prospects, so Numonyx could only bet on PCM — PCM combined NOR's fast random reads with NAND's high-capacity storage, and in theory could replace both. In February 2008 Intel announced delivery of its first PCM prototype, Alverstone, at 128 megabit and 90 nanometers.

13:33 Mobile PCM was swept away in one wave by 3D NAND
PCM's entry strategy was to attack the mobile market, replacing the NOR flash that stores boot code while also storing data. In 2009 Samsung announced a 512 megabit PRAM at 60 nanometers, saying that paired with DRAM it could save more than 20% in power. Micron acquired Numonyx in 2010 for about $1.2 billion in stock, and in July 2012 finally shipped 1 gigabit PCM at 45 nanometers, which Nokia put into its Asha feature phones. But in August 2013 Samsung announced mass production of 24-layer 3D NAND, and 3D NAND then set off the steepest cost-decline curve in semiconductor history, and mobile PCM's most compelling rationale was gone. In January 2014 Micron announced it was pulling out of mobile PCM.

17:38 Intel and Micron were split on Optane's positioning from the start
In July 2018 Intel and Micron agreed to a friendly breakup, going their separate ways after completing joint development of second-generation 3D XPoint. The disagreement was over product direction: Intel initially aimed Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops, hoping to spread wafer costs across volume; Micron wanted to go straight into the data center. Jon Carter hinted back in 2016 that consumer systems did not really need 3D XPoint's low latency, non-volatility and endurance, or at least not enough to pay four to five times the price of NAND for them. In October 2018 Micron announced it would pay $1.5 billion to buy Intel's half of the IM Flash plant in Utah, and Intel shifted to producing it itself.

22:47 Putting Optane into the data center meant redoing motherboards and software
In April 2019 the first DIMM-form-factor Optane DC Persistent Memory went on sale, four years after 3D XPoint was announced, and it required matching Xeon processors, chipsets and motherboards. It had two modes: Memory Mode pooled Optane and DRAM into a single volatile memory pool, worked out of the box, but its value depended on DRAM price swings; App Direct Mode was the genuinely valuable mode, letting software write persistent data into Optane so it was still there after a reboot. Restarting an Oracle or SAP database normally takes over an hour to reload data from SSDs or hard drives, and Optane could eliminate that. One imprecise but directionally useful test showed a 12.5x improvement. But App Direct Mode required programmers to rethink data consistency.

24:51 Only 40% of 582 proofs of concept used the mode that actually mattered
In 2020 Intel updated Optane adoption, saying there were 582 proofs of concept in the pipeline, with SAP HANA and Oracle Exadata the main users and the rest mostly in high-performance computing, infrastructure and some AI analytics. But only 40% used the more valuable App Direct Mode. Intel said it believed the industry would eventually adopt that mode, but it might take years. In the same period Intel announced the sale of its 3D NAND business to SK hynix for $9 billion, with Optane not included in the deal, which looked like an endorsement but also let people infer that Optane's implied loss in 2020 was more than $500 million.

25:52 After Micron left, Optane had only a single supplier
In March 2021 Micron announced it was immediately stopping 3D XPoint development, saying the Utah plant had long suffered from underutilization and dragged $400 million a year off the company, and the plant was later sold to Texas Instruments. Micron attributed the decision to 3D NAND prices continuing to fall, and to the hard changes data centers and applications would have to make to take full advantage of the product. Micron pivoted to betting on the open-standard interface CXL, because machine-learning systems made Micron realize that not just CPUs needed more memory — GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs did too. Micron's public exit severely weakened Optane: customers could rely only on Intel as a single source, and Optane was a proprietary technology. In July 2022 Intel quietly announced the shutdown of the Optane business on its earnings call.
