He also says the lack of rules and accountability in the social media era actually led to a lack of innovation in ‘how to build products safer from the start’.

24:57 Tolerating domestic monopoly for external competition is wrong
Cantor's framework: promote fierce, dynamic competition within the US, including foreign companies, because America is a market economy, and the chance of success incentivizes people to try new things, invest capital, and make good products. He says the idea that ‘we need domestic monopoly to compete abroad’ is fundamentally opposed to the American way of life — America's founding itself was a revolt against British monopoly over life's necessities. He acknowledges legitimate questions, such as how to handle foreign below-cost dumping, which this administration is raising; he mentions an 80s case he read with law students: Japanese companies were accused of cartelizing TV prices in Japan, then cross-subsidizing below-cost pricing in the US to crush domestic American manufacturers, and the Supreme Court at the time used an absurd set of economics to find this didn't constitute an antitrust violation. But he says the way to handle this isn't to allow the domestic market to be monopolized.

28:04 NVIDIA's circular investments should be scrutinized
The host asks on behalf of the most skeptical listeners: NVIDIA has circularly invested in all these companies, they're effectively already coordinated; the products liability theory will fall flat because OpenAI will never sue Hugging Face, and NVIDIA just bought Hugging Face and is OpenAI's largest investor — shouldn't all this be broken apart? Cantor says ‘someone should be looking at these questions’, which is exactly what they started doing in office: draw some lines, you can't buy whichever company you want or invest in whichever company you want, competition has to be competition, and within the boundaries you can compete as much as you like. He criticizes this administration for allowing a few companies to reach dominant, oligopolistic, or monopolistic positions to ‘beat China’, but he asks ‘what does beating China even mean’ — if China has advanced bots invading American companies and government servers, that's a national security, geopolitical, international relations problem, and shouldn't be solved by domestic monopoly, especially when these monopolists are loyal to shareholders rather than the public interest.

item.title: A Big Year for M&A, but Only 2% of Companies Are Actually Using AI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-19-oddlots-ai-并购大年-但企业真正用起来的只有-2/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-19-oddlots-ai-并购大年-但企业真正用起来的只有-2/
item.description: Gene Sykes, Goldman Sachs' co-head of M&A, says this is the biggest M&A year in history, driven by AI infrastructure; but only 2% of companies are seeing AI lift EPS in their reported results.
item.content:encoded:
Gene Sykes, Goldman Sachs' co-head of M&A, says this is the biggest M&A year in history, driven by AI infrastructure; but only 2% of companies are seeing AI lift EPS in their reported results.

The first half is about Olympic sponsorship and transportation details, the second half is where M&A, AI adoption rates and media asset pricing come in; medium information density.

4:07 The Olympics is an order of magnitude bigger than the World Cup
Gene Sykes gives the comparison: the World Cup was held across Mexico, the United States and Canada, with 104 matches, 16 stadiums and roughly 600 athletes. The Los Angeles Olympics and Paralympics together will have 17,000 athletes, about 900 medal events, and 15 million tickets sold across the two — the World Cup sold only 6.5 million. His claim is that the Olympics covers roughly 90% of the sports world you can imagine. That scale difference puts the organizational complexity on an entirely different level.

5:07 Los Angeles doesn't have to build a single venue
On the so-called "first privately funded Olympics," Sykes' explanation is: there is no government money to run the Games, and the federal government only plays a role in security and related logistics, because 206 countries will send teams. What makes this possible is that Southern California already has the best sports infrastructure in the world — the venues and arenas are all there, nothing needs to be built. The athletes' village doesn't need to be built either: everyone stays in UCLA dorms — UCLA normally houses more students than the athletes needed during the Olympics. This is the key to why these Games are easier to plan and execute.

11:17 Media rights were sold a decade in advance
Part of the Olympics' money is "pre-baked": the International Olympic Committee sells the media rights for all Olympics many years ahead of time, NBC is the U.S. rights holder, and the contract already runs to 2036 — by which point nobody even knows where the Olympics will be held. The U.S. rights fee is $1.5 billion or more per Games. The IOC also sells sponsorships to companies like Coca-Cola, Visa and Samsung. Then the domestic organizing committee sells another round, and for Los Angeles that went to Starbucks, Uber and Google. Sykes says corporate interest is enormous, because everyone believes this will be the biggest event in world history.

14:19 This is the biggest M&A year in history
Sykes says this is the biggest M&A year in world history, and by a wide margin. The previous peak was 2021, and that was inflated by COVID. Over the past few years, 40% of the M&A market was sales of private-equity-owned companies; this year that share has fallen to 30%, because more substantive demand has appeared — around AI's impact on the economy, every industry is going through the same thing, natural resources and power generation alike, because they are building AI infrastructure. There is a huge boom in semiconductor technology and semiconductor M&A, because everyone wants to own proprietary semiconductor technology.

16:20 80% of startups end up being acquired
Sykes' judgment is: every startup, even an AI company, has to think clearly about what its endgame is, and 80% of startups end their lives by selling themselves to someone else. This is both the calculation in the founder's head and the source of economic return for the VCs behind them — you have to figure out how what you build helps another piece of the puzzle. The remaining 20% can become durably independent companies, either because they have something completely differentiated or because they simply can't find a buyer. He cites SpaceX as an example: in a market that already had plenty of incumbents, it did something different, and those incumbents were constrained by the regulatory environment, so SpaceX chose to challenge it.

17:23 Anthropic and OpenAI are too big for anyone to buy
Sykes says Anthropic and OpenAI will obviously become independent companies, because they are almost too big for anyone to buy. That's the other side: if a company gets too big, it means it has succeeded very well, but you have to have enough confidence that they own a durable platform. Tracey follows up: will we someday read in the risk factors of an S-1, "we believe there is a non-trivial probability that our technology will wipe out all of humanity"? Sykes says lawyers would probably say you need to protect yourself and make sure disclosure is complete, so that kind of big, crazy, scary thing will definitely show up in S-1 language.

19:23 This infrastructure build is funded from free cash flow
On the analogy between AI infrastructure and the TMT bubble, Sykes says there's no way to know how big the market will be, or whether it will be overbuilt relative to real demand five or six years from now — the answer is "we just don't know." But he points to one key difference: in the first TMT internet buildout of 2000 and 2001, the money came mainly from VCs; this buildout is funded by the world's most successful large technology platforms, which until this year had hundreds of billions of dollars in free cash flow. That's an astonishing reversal.

20:25 Only 2% are actually seeing AI lift EPS
Joe offers a theory: enterprise AI adoption is basically zero. Sykes says they just ran the analysis, and it's 2% — meaning the companies that say in their financial reports that their use of AI has had a positive impact on EPS, currently only 2%. He distinguishes several levels: maybe 20% to 30% of companies have implemented a strategy of using AI across their businesses; while employees each having a ChatGPT or Claude subscription and using it as "glorified search" doesn't count as meaningful adoption. He uses Goldman itself as an example: there are a lot of prompts using AI to do things, and the youngest employees are "AI natives," doing things a year ago you couldn't have imagined.

item.title: Anti-Data Centres Is Almost Entirely a Chinese Psyop
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-19-twentyvc-反数据中心几乎全是中国的心理战/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-19-twentyvc-反数据中心几乎全是中国的心理战/
item.description: The American left and right are both fighting new data centres, and Thomas Sohmers thinks it is almost entirely a Chinese psyop — China is building at full speed while the West slows itself down with regulation.
item.content:encoded:
The American left and right are both fighting new data centres, and Thomas Sohmers thinks it is almost entirely a Chinese psyop — China is building at full speed while the West slows itself down with regulation.

The first half is macro judgment on anti-data-centre sentiment, energy and debt; the second half is hard mechanics on KV cache, quantization and context length. High information density, but it takes a little patience.

5:06 Training is compute-bound; inference is memory-bound
Thomas lays out the fundamental difference between training and inference clearly: in training you already have the entire corpus, so you can feed tokens in massively parallel — it is essentially a compute-bound problem, which is why export-control frameworks mostly target FLOPS. But inference is generative: you do not know the token five words ahead, so you must generate one at a time in sequence, and every token generated requires reading the weights again. That makes it an extremely memory-bound problem, impossible to parallelise the way training is. This difference dictates that inference hardware is designed on completely different logic from training chips.

7:08 Compute rose 120x, memory bandwidth only 17x
Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the FLOPS of a single NVIDIA GPU rose about 120x, but memory bandwidth rose only 17x. Thomas says this is the real manifestation of the memory wall: the ratio of compute to memory bandwidth has diverged enormously, and the further out you go, the worse the memory-bound problem gets. One reason is that SRAM cells have scaled far more slowly than ordinary transistors over the past fifteen years, and the architecture has barely changed in thirty or forty years. Another reason is incentive — in the CNN era of the 2010s, models were essentially compute-bound, you just threw more FLOPS at them, and nobody had any incentive to solve memory bandwidth.

11:16 The margin on selling cached tokens is ‘obscene’
Thomas says the cost of processing a cached token is roughly one-thousandth of recomputing and generating that token, so the margin on selling cached tokens is absurdly high. Nearly every provider charges a higher rate for cache than for ordinary input tokens, then a lower rate on reads; users feel it is cheap, but providers earn an ‘obscene margin’ on cache reads. He notes Anthropic's API business has been reported at 80 points of gross margin, and he is not surprised — getting 80 points in any industry is hard. He thinks those margins will compress with competition, and that if OpenAI and Anthropic stopped training, they would be hugely profitable overnight.

21:45 Anti-data-centre sentiment is almost entirely a Chinese psyop
Thomas says the left and right have now reached near-consensus against data centres, which in his eyes is the most terrifying thing in politics, and he believes it is almost entirely a Chinese psyop. He rebuts the water-consumption argument: an in-and-out burger uses more water than the largest data centre in America, a golf course is orders of magnitude higher still, and these data centres are closed-loop liquid-cooled systems that in many cases do not want to use water at all. His argument: China itself is building at full speed, adding gigawatts of generation capacity, and flattening homes and cutting power to residents for training capacity, while the West slows itself down on the basis of false information.

25:54 Data centres will not take residents' electricity
Thomas says utilities have to provide a quote for energy availability, and that quote is already baked into everyone's costs and capabilities, so a data centre cannot possibly pull power from electricity already allocated to residents — it is impossible. Moreover, the data centres being built today come with their own generation capacity covering their own use and even more, but are simply not allowed to connect to the grid — if they were connected, they would actually lower everyone's electricity price. He also points out that utilities are lobbying against new generation capacity, because market forces would let more capacity push prices down, which is good for consumers but not for utilities.

35:21 KV cache turns quadratic cost into linear storage
Thomas explains the mechanics of KV cache: the Transformer originally recomputed all previous tokens for every token generated, until it was realised you do not need to redo the parts already processed, so the K and V matrices are stored. The key point is that under attention, the compute per token grows quadratically with sequence length, while storing K and V grows only linearly. So KV cache trades storage for computation that gets expensive fast. But storage is itself complexity: every user has a unique KV cache, and you have to decide how long to keep it and how to manage it across a large system.

38:31 96% of agentic coding tokens are cache hits
Thomas mentions SemiAnalysis's agent X benchmark, based on a large number of cloud code sessions with dozens to hundreds of turns, plus sub-agents. They found that in these real traced code-generation, agentic coding sessions, about 96% of tokens are cache hits. That means if you know a workload has an extremely high cache rate, the importance of cache retrieval rises sharply, because those caches become very large. He gives an example: GPT-4 was leaked as a 1.8 trillion parameter model, roughly 900 GB of model weights after quantization; if Claude is 10 trillion parameters, that is about 5 TB of weights. But under long context, a single user session can reach the 100 GB scale, so 50 users' contexts exceed the model weights themselves.

57:17 Chinese labs used algorithms to route around memory export controls
Thomas says context length is heading from today's million tokens to 10x and beyond, which is very hard under quadratic memory cost. Algorithmic progress over the past year has been interesting, able to further reduce the storage and compute context requires, and Chinese model labs have innovated a lot here. He cites DeepSeek V3: because export controls limit chips with the highest memory capacity and FLOPS, they innovated methods that do not need those chips, using multi-head latent attention to greatly shrink KV cache size at the cost of spending more FLOPS. He says the major US labs, as far as he knows, have not used MLA, but that will change in the future.

item.title: Carrots Haven't Lost Their Nutrients — What Changed Is the Zinc and Iron in Wheat
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-19-moreorless-胡萝卜没变没营养-变的是小麦的锌和铁/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-19-moreorless-胡萝卜没变没营养-变的是小麦的锌和铁/
item.description: The popular claim that depleted soil is making vegetables less nutritious has no data behind it; what is actually documented is the dilution effect in high-yield dwarf wheat, where zinc has fallen by about half.
item.content:encoded:
The popular claim that depleted soil is making vegetables less nutritious has no data behind it; what is actually documented is the dilution effect in high-yield dwarf wheat, where zinc has fallen by about half.

8 minutes, medium information density. Suited to anyone who wants to know whether popular claims about "food losing its nutrients" have any evidence at all. The conclusion is clear but not exactly颠覆 — not exactly颠覆.

0:00 The popular claim that a listener's letter sets off
The episode starts with a listener, Sarah, who read a line from Dr Karen Rajan on BBC News: we know soil is not as nutrient-dense as it was decades ago, so a carrot in the 1950s was far more nutritious than a carrot in 2026. Host Tim Harford breaks that into two testable propositions: whether fruits and vegetables really have lost nutrients, and whether soil really has been depleted. The answers to those two are not the same, and the episode handles them separately.

1:02 Nutrition databases were never built for comparing across time
Robin Miles, a former senior scientist at the Canadian Food and Nutrition Bureau, points out that the conclusions about "big drops in calcium and iron" mostly come from nutrient composition databases. Those databases are designed for registered dietitians building menus; sample sizes are usually small, and analytical methods have kept changing over the years. Using them for a scientific comparison across decades is not appropriate. Robin says the statistically more rigorous studies conclude that nutrient levels in crops have broadly not declined.

3:05 The real decline in a 180-year wheat experiment
The Broadbalk experiment at Rothamsted Research has grown wheat since 1843, preserving samples of soil, crops and even fertiliser — it is the oldest experiment in the world. Steve McGrath says nutrient concentrations did not change for a long time, until around the 1960s or 70s, when some nutrients began to fall sharply: zinc down 50%, iron, magnesium and copper down 20% to 30%. This is the hardest set of numbers in the whole piece, and the only part of the "nutrient decline" claim that holds up.

4:12 The cause of the decline is yield, not soil
McGrath attributes the decline to the higher grain share brought by dwarf varieties: the dwarf wheat promoted by Norman Borlaug in the Green Revolution sharply raised the ratio of grain to straw, and as the harvest index rose, the concentrations of zinc, iron, magnesium and copper in the grain fell. In his words, more carbohydrate was packed in for higher yield, the nutrients did not keep up, and the concentration was diluted. That is the dilution effect. The mechanism is not fully understood — it may also involve how nutrients are taken up from the short stem or the roots into the grain — but he is confident it was not caused by changes in soil nutrients.

5:15 Soil nutrients have actually risen
McGrath's team analysed soil nutrients on that experimental plot over 180 years; concentrations had not fallen but had risen somewhat. He gives two reasons why soil nutrients could not have been lost on a large scale: first, there is almost no data on how soil changes over time, so the claim that "the nutrients all disappeared from the soil" has nothing to stand on; second, most of the micronutrients he studies cling tightly to soil particles and are not soluble, so they do not wash away with water, and he sees no mechanism for a large decline.

6:18 Soil degradation is serious, but that is not nutrients being washed away
The episode deliberately separates two things: soil degradation is indeed a serious global problem, including carbon loss, salinisation, acidification, contamination by certain elements, and wind and water erosion; but that is a different matter from "nutrients being washed away and making vegetables less nutritious." McGrath says there is almost no data supporting the latter. This distinction is the key to the whole episode — acknowledging that soil has problems is not the same as accepting that popular causal chain.

7:21 Rice and oats probably have the same problem, but nobody knows how much
Back to the original question: the claim that carrots are less nutritious than in 1950 lacks good evidence, and so does the claim that soil nutrient density has fallen. But some important nutrients in wheat really have declined, and McGrath thinks the same process very likely happens in other staple crops, such as rice, barley and oats, because they too have been bred to raise yield per plant. Which crops exactly, and by how much, is not currently known. The advice at the end of the episode is plain: eat as varied and balanced a diet as you can.

item.title: Treating service as a cost center is the biggest misjudgment in business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-twist-把服务当成本中心-是商业上最大的误判/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-twist-把服务当成本中心-是商业上最大的误判/
item.description: Products and brands will always be surpassed; the only long-term moat is making people feel seen — and that can be systematized like dropping a coin in a parking meter, no budget required, just care.
item.content:encoded:
Products and brands will always be surpassed; the only long-term moat is making people feel seen — and that can be systematized like dropping a coin in a parking meter, no budget required, just care.

Medium information density. The first half is a collection of hospitality cases; the second half, on fair use of AI and running a restaurant, is more worth hearing.

4:05 Product moats get filled in sooner or later
Will Guidara's judgment: no matter how good your product or how strong your brand, time will prove that someone builds a better product and a stronger brand — maybe with more capital, more creativity, or simply better than you. So the only competitive advantage that lasts comes from hospitality — continuously and generously investing in relationships. He acknowledges that anyone who has achieved even a little success did it by being "unreasonable" in their investment in product and service; he is only arguing that you shouldn't save your best effort for the product alone, but also invest it in "how people feel."

17:16 Hospitality can be systematized, not left to flashes of inspiration
One-off surprises like the hot dog or the first dance are hard to scale and can't be forced, or they look calculated. But Guidara says these are evidence that "you can systematize hospitality": do pattern recognition, find the moments that recur, then write "how to respond gracefully" into the process. For example, guests often had to put coins in the parking meter, so the rule became: every time it happens, go put the coins in for them. Once hospitality is written into the system, the team actually gets inspired to be more hospitable — because after putting coins in for a guest and seeing the gratitude on their face, it's a high you want to experience again and again.

24:18 No airline has ever built a business around crying babies
Guidara points to a gap he calls "criminal": flying across the US with a one-year-old is excruciating, yet no airline has ever handed earplugs to the surrounding passengers, offered parents any help, or done anything but tell you there's no milk. He calls this a failure of pattern recognition — a scenario that recurs and that everyone knows about, yet nobody catches it. Jason adds: this requires the top to hand down a budget, say $250 per person per month to spend on guests, and let the front line decide how to use it; employees will love the job for it, and guests will become loyal.

34:24 When a pet dies, Chewy sends flowers to the door
Chewy's auto-subscription dog food has one moment that is bound to happen: after the dog dies, the owner's first instinct isn't to cancel the subscription — they wait until the next bag arrives, remember, then call to ask for a return. Chewy's response is fixed: they can't take it back, but they'll refund it and suggest donating the food; within a day or two, flowers arrive at the house. Guidara's read: this person will get another dog, and the dog food will only ever come from Chewy, with no other brand even considered. That's pattern recognition, recurring moments, and systematized kindness all holding true at once.

36:24 They stole his story, then made him a producer
The Forks episode of The Bear is basically taken from this book, rewriting the hot dog story as a deep dish pizza story. The show gave Guidara the cut long before it aired to confirm he was okay with it; he is close to that group and later became a co-producer on seasons three and four. Jason uses this to bring up AI and copyright: being technically able to do something doesn't mean you should, and legality is only the lowest bar of morality. Guidara's landing point — they could have made him feel robbed, but chose to make him part of it instead.

53:31 Ending tipping requires two preconditions to hold at once
Guidara eliminated tipping at Eleven Madison Park, which he calls the most successful tipping elimination ever; but after he sold the restaurant, the new owners added tipping back, because the restaurant wasn't doing as well as before. His conclusion: eliminating tipping demands that you run the business extremely well, or it backfires. Two preconditions must be true — demand is high enough that guests don't mind the price increase; and you must stay consistently full, because you're covering tips for the team, and one slow night means you lose money outright. He also says they folded the service charge directly into the prix fixe price, and guests sometimes insisted on pressing cash into their hands; the team's favorite game was figuring out how to slip it back into a pocket or bag before they left.

56:33 On scalping restaurant reservations, he says flatly: it's wrong
On the secondary market for reservations at places like Eleven Madison, Guidara's attitude is "I hated it." The reason: he priced the experience as high as possible while still offering tremendous value, and if a guest pays someone else $200 before even walking in, he can no longer deliver matching revenue and value. He admits the logic is contradictory: someone else made money, you paid voluntarily, so what right does he have to stop it? But he still thinks it's wrong; he adds that if he were still running a restaurant, there would be plenty of other things more worth his time and energy.

1:03:36 New York commuter rail hides a minute of grace
A recent newsletter from Guidara is about commuter rail like Metro-North and Amtrak: the system has "a minute of grace" built in — the timetable says 11:45 departure, but it always actually leaves at 11:46, to leave room for whoever sprints through the door at the last second. He says that ever since he learned this, he started looking for his own "minutes of grace" in dealings with other companies and his own. Jason's echo is direct: not wasting time at an airport gate or on a train is the lifelong optimization of every New Yorker.

item.title: Pacing Is a PR Mistake; Cyberattacks Are the Real Risk
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-a16z-ai-放慢节奏是公关失误-网络攻击才是真风险/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-a16z-ai-放慢节奏是公关失误-网络攻击才是真风险/
item.description: Frontier labs packaging safety as pacing pleases no one; the real emergency is CVE weaponization compressing from years to minutes, while enterprises still have no agents, only faster search.
item.content:encoded:
Frontier labs packaging safety as pacing pleases no one; the real emergency is CVE weaponization compressing from years to minutes, while enterprises still have no agents, only faster search.

The Databricks CEO lays out pacing, the RSI test, the cyberattack curve, enterprise agent adoption and cost governance in one pass — the ontology and harness mechanics in the back half are the most valuable part.

0:00 Pacing is a PR mistake, not a safety strategy
Ali argues that frontier labs packaging "safety" as "pacing" is a textbook PR mistake. Pacing is orthogonal to safety — you can build weapons slowly, and that's no different from building weapons; and these companies have been running at full speed and buying more compute, so nobody believes the pacing talk. The result pleases no one: doomers don't think it's a pause, and policy people don't think you know how to do it. What they should be saying, he argues, is "secure the frontier," not "pace the frontier."

12:24 RSI only counts if four conditions hold at once
Ali gives four criteria for judging whether recursive self-improvement is happening, and all four must hold simultaneously: the next generation of models requires fewer resources (GPUs), takes less training time, is smarter/more accurate, and these three things can repeat over and over. If any one fails, the system self-limits — for instance, with constant resources it hits a hardware wall. He stresses that "software writing software" is already happening today, with more than 90% of software at Databricks written by AI, but that is not the same as superintelligence.

15:24 The cost curve for frontier training runs the other way
Sarah points out that the compute bar for training frontier models keeps rising — from 100 million to 1 billion, and now roughly 5 to 10 billion. Ali adds: there are only one or two such training runs a year, and they flatly violate those four criteria — they need more resources, more people, are more fragile, and require building data centers, networking and fault tolerance. Several have blown up, and failure means burning enormous sums. So the reality is "slower, more fragile, harder" — not "faster, cheaper, smarter."

24:40 Vulnerability weaponization went from two or three years to hours
Ali gives this curve: in 2018 and 2019, a CVE took roughly two to three years from disclosure to weaponization; by 2022 it was down to eight or nine months; from 2022 to now it has compressed to essentially hours, almost no time at all. The reason is that data and AI are merging with the cybersecurity market — companies run large numbers of agents internally, generating massive logs and traces, and the volume of data that needs analyzing is orders of magnitude larger than a year or two ago.

32:44 Say AI will destroy the world, then ask if you want IPO allocation
Ali concedes two things can be true at once: some people really are scared by AI risk, and some people want regulation to "pace us" — because slowing down benefits them. People can always reconcile self-interest and fear into a harmonious whole in their heads, he says. The industry has long had this marketing play: the moment a new model is trained, shout about how terrifyingly good it is, and the world's attention arrives. But he also gives the other side: the time from CVE to actual weaponized exploit went from years to minutes in three or four years, and cyberattacks are real. So "scary" is both a genuine risk and excellent marketing.

39:50 Enterprises have no agents, only faster search
Ali polled the room live: he asked how many in the audience were managing hundreds or thousands of agents coordinating and negotiating with each other, and almost no hands went up. What most enterprises use is Microsoft Copilot, essentially a chatbot — "a very, very glorified, efficient Google search." Coding is the only scenario that has truly landed, and even there the ROI is debatable. He thinks the reason isn't that models aren't smart enough, but that models lack the organization's internal context: they haven't sat in every meeting, don't know what's in everyone's head, don't know the processes. Every organization has a few employees who know everything, and when you tap them on the shoulder you think, "what if he quits?" Pour that context into today's frontier models and you get enormous productivity — and that doesn't require a smarter model.

47:01 Ontology is that employee who's been there five years
Ali explains ontology with a concrete picture: two people equally smart, equally hardworking, with identical educational backgrounds — one on their first day, one who's been there five years. The difference is that the latter knows how the organization runs, who people are, how things get done — "don't look at the org chart, don't ask that guy, he can't get anything done." That is ontology: tacit knowledge scattered across everyone's heads. He contrasts it with the state of agents today: the agentic loop looks up resources one at a time, like Google crawling ten sites live on every search, taking ten minutes, and then handing you ten blue links — expensive, slow and bad. Google's answer was the index, and AI also needs that index computed offline, only harder — because of permission constraints, since data I can access isn't necessarily data you can access, and the object types go far beyond web pages.

56:08 Same model, different harness, twice the cost
Databricks' answer is a full cost-governance stack: Unity Gateway provides token capacity for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Grok and open-source models, sets budget caps and alerts by person and by group, does cost forecasting analytics, and adds intelligent routing to switch to cheaper models when nearing budget or when the question is simple. Ali gives a concrete number: the same model, the same version, just a different harness, and actual cost can differ by nearly 2x. Their in-house harness is called Omnigent, which can multiplex across different harnesses. The result is token usage keeps climbing while AI cost stays roughly flat.

item.title: AI demand still runs ahead of supply, but the compute bottleneck is turning into a political problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-mastersinbiz-ai-需求仍跑在供给前面-但算力瓶颈正在变成政治问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-mastersinbiz-ai-需求仍跑在供给前面-但算力瓶颈正在变成政治问题/
item.description: Glen Kacher of Light Street sees AI as a 15-to-20-year rebuild of the computing stack, and only a third of the first leg is done; the real risk is not over-investment in CapEx but power and local politics slowing construction.
item.content:encoded:
Glen Kacher of Light Street sees AI as a 15-to-20-year rebuild of the computing stack, and only a third of the first leg is done; the real risk is not over-investment in CapEx but power and local politics slowing construction.

An investor running a tech hedge fund in the heart of Silicon Valley strings AI compute, semiconductors, open-source models and the power bottleneck into one investable chain of reasoning, at high information density.

7:16 Buy only the best company, never the second or third
Over 13 years at Integral Capital, Kacher made 46 private investments, and the lesson he drew is: do not buy the second- or third-best company in an industry, always buy the best one you can get. The reason is that in tech the leader takes two-thirds of the market, the number two gets 20% to 25% at most, and everyone else fights over scraps. Higher margins plus a dominant share compound the lead. But he also concedes that incumbents in tech get disrupted, and disruption usually comes not from big companies but from small ones — AI and the semiconductors behind AI are exactly the test case for that rule.

8:17 Nvidia's moat is underappreciated
Kacher says many people assume Nvidia will lose its roughly 85% share of AI accelerators, and the shift to inference does give competitors an opening. But he thinks the market currently underestimates Nvidia's own capacity to innovate. He describes the evolution of inference chips as an alphabet progression from CPU to FPU to GPU to XPU, where X stands for the unknown: Google has TPU, there is Trainium and other vendors' approaches, and Nvidia itself bought the Grok inference line. He judges that inference will ultimately be a bigger market than training, so there will be many chip forms and many opportunities to innovate.

21:51 Four semiconductor companies are 40% of the portfolio
TSMC, Nvidia, Broadcom and AMD make up roughly 40% of Light Street's public holdings, a highly concentrated portfolio. Kacher's logic: concentrate capital where innovation is densest, and right now the densest place is the core of AI accelerated computing. Nvidia has more than 80% of the GPU networking market and AMD is catching up; as agentic AI becomes the next growth driver, AMD has a unique edge because it is one of the two big players in both desktop and server CPUs; Broadcom has built TPUs for Google for years and now has opportunities with big players like OpenAI; TSMC fabs for all three, so it wins no matter who wins, an almost oligopolistic or even monopolistic position.

26:01 Open-source models are fighting a price war
Kacher thinks the battle between Anthropic and OpenAI is happening in real time, and that Google remains a player thanks to Gemini and its search distribution advantage, so it cannot be ruled out. But the battlefield that is really emerging is open-source models: they are free, can be downloaded to run on local hardware, or run on someone else's commoditized hardware in the cloud, competing directly with the two big companies' expensive frontier models. He judges that early signals show both approaches have their place. He also points to the regulatory problem: open-source models can be put inside your own software and tuned to your needs, and regulators actually have few options, because these models are already out in the wild.

33:14 Someone was saying GPUs should do AI back in 2005
Kacher recalls that while at Integral, Bill Joy, a partner at Kleiner Perkins, mentioned a group of engineers at Caltech using GPUs for early AI computation, around 2005 or 2006, and Bill Joy's conclusion was that GPUs would be the chip architecture best suited to AI computation. It stayed in his head. Later, on every visit to Nvidia, Jensen would talk about AI, but at the time AI was only a tiny end market for Nvidia, and crypto mattered far more. In the second half of 2022 the crypto crash and AI's takeoff happened at the same time, the market was more focused on crypto and pushed the stock down, which gave them the chance to build a position in Nvidia.

45:36 The giants are not over-investing, they are catching up
Faced with the challenge that AI will be over-provisioned like fiber, Kacher's answer is: Amazon, Microsoft and Google are building the compute stack in partnership with Anthropic and OpenAI, and the question is how far ahead of demand they are planning. His judgment is that today they are not ahead, they are behind and catching up. Bears expect them to over-invest, but that is not happening today. He concedes there are real bottlenecks, including the memory companies and TSMC, which cannot invest as fast as they would like even if they wanted to, so demand today still runs far ahead of supply, and the pessimism around AI is misplaced.

52:47 A fifteen-year cycle, and only a third of it is done
Kacher likens AI to the shift from client-server to internet architecture, a computing cycle that happens roughly every 15 to 25 years. The old technology was a search-then-retrieve model, with data sitting in databases; AI generates a custom answer to your question and your data on every use, and is far more compute-intensive. The rhythm he gives: infrastructure development takes roughly 5 to 10 years, years 6 to 16 are when the platform or operating system takes shape, and years 11 to 21 are when applications become the main venue for enterprise investment and innovation. By that framework, roughly a third of the first leg is done now, and the whole cycle is at least 15 to 20 years.

53:48 Power and local politics have become the new bottleneck
Kacher treats political resistance to data centers as a real risk: any bottleneck that slows technology adoption is a problem. He says it is not a big problem today, but it is an emerging one. His solution is that the industry has to explain itself proactively: Northern Virginia, as the data center capital of the world, has brought the area tax revenue and blue-collar demand for electricians, plumbers and construction workers, a shot in the arm for the economy. He mentions a data center project in San Mateo that plans to put Bloom Energy natural gas fuel cells behind the meter, with almost no emissions and almost no noise, and residents still opposed it because they had "heard data centers are bad." He sees this as an education problem, requiring project-by-project explanations of energy, jobs and tax revenue, from local to national.

item.title: The Pizza Tracker: We've Been Trained to Pay for Fake Progress Bars
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-planetmoney-披萨追踪器-我们被驯化成愿意为假进度条买单/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-planetmoney-披萨追踪器-我们被驯化成愿意为假进度条买单/
item.description: Domino's pizza tracker started as an internal management tool, then became a global app standard. It works because it turns waiting into visible work; and once companies discovered we love watching progress bars, they started faking them.
item.content:encoded:
Domino's pizza tracker started as an internal management tool, then became a global app standard. It works because it turns waiting into visible work; and once companies discovered we love watching progress bars, they started faking them.

Medium information density, but the second half about 'deliberate slowdowns' and 'fake progress bars' is valuable. Suitable for listeners interested in product design and consumer psychology.

2:07 The 30-minute guarantee sold control, not speed
Domino's once promised delivery in 30 minutes or it's free. This guarantee made drivers speed, leading to deaths and lawsuits, and it was eventually cancelled. But David Halbenstricker has a theory: the guarantee was popular not just because it was fast, but because it gave customers a sense of control. In the early 2000s, Domino's commissioned a study and found that customers' psychology after ordering pizza is a rollercoaster: the peak is at ordering, then it slides downhill—'Where's my pizza? Did they lose my order?' No matter the actual wait, what customers hate is the process of waiting.

8:16 Internal tools had to work first, before customer-facing ones
Executives didn't initially want to build a pizza tracker because tracking every pizza at every store was too time-consuming and seemed like a gimmick. What they were truly obsessed with was 'out-the-door time.' A UK franchisee used a monitor to display out-the-door times from five to ten nearby stores, letting them compete, and gave cash rewards to top-ranked stores. After David's boss visited the UK, he had David replicate the system in the US. David connected each store's out-the-door time to a central system, creating a real-time dashboard. The CEO said it was the thing that most drove performance during his tenure.

11:25 The tracker was a byproduct of the internal system
David and his colleagues realized they already had a system tracking every pizza, so they decided to 'hitch a ride' and build a customer-facing tracker. In 2006, most people didn't have smartphones; FedEx, UPS, and Amazon could track packages, but on a scale of days, not minutes. Real-time pizza tracking was entirely new. The designer's interface looked like a horizontal thermometer, from order, prep, bake, box, to delivery; each completed step turned the next segment red. When David saw the design, he said: 'This is a hot dog. We're a pizza company, why is there a hot dog?' But executives liked it and decided to launch before the Super Bowl.

15:36 Designers use the pizza tracker as a meeting prop
Shuya Gong was a design director at IDEO and later taught design at Harvard. In the mid-2010s, she consulted for many companies and found one of the most effective meeting openers was to order a pizza on the spot, project the tracker on a big screen, and ask the client: 'How do you feel right now?' She said you can feel the anxiety rise or fall in your body, feel reassurance and groundedness. Then you can ask: which parts do you want your users to feel when using your product? The pizza tracker became a shorthand in her design circle: whenever a client involved waiting, they'd say 'they need a pizza tracker.'

17:39 The tracker creates a 'labor illusion'
Shuya said one reason the pizza tracker is popular is that as shopping experiences become more digital, the tracker replicates an important part of the physical world—watching others work. Online experiences lack this visibility, so people get impatient more easily. Researchers found that reminding customers of the labor behind a product makes them value it more, calling it the 'labor illusion.' Shuya also mentioned a more mysterious mechanism: the tracker changes our perception of time. Like walking somewhere, the return trip feels shorter because it's familiar and has landmarks. The pizza tracker gives us familiar routes and landmarks—pizza being made, on the road, being delivered—making the wait feel shorter.

19:47 Banks deliberately slow transfers to create fake waiting
In the mid-2010s, Shuya worked with banks and fintech companies and found their problem was the opposite of Domino's: customers weren't used to transfers being too fast. Two computers talk, confirm the amount, and the money is gone—no roads to cross, no cheese to melt. But for people used to money taking a while to arrive, instant arrival 'feels suspicious.' So companies deliberately slow down the 'money tracker,' not giving real-time feedback but adding a buffer to make you wait. Shuya said this is intentionally slowing down time, adding meaningful friction so you feel the seriousness and weight of the transfer while waiting. The host asked: isn't this advising lying to customers? Shuya said she prefers to understand it as 'curating the experience,' adding back the physicality that existed in traditional experiences to make people comfortable.

21:48 TurboTax and Uber progress bars may be fake
TurboTax shows an animation during tax filing saying 'We're checking your deductions and credits.' But a few years ago someone checked the code and found the animation is the same for everyone, in all situations, and takes the same time. The question is: does TurboTax want to reassure us during the terrifying tax process, or use the labor illusion to make us feel paying a large sum is worth it? Uber is similar: the host repeatedly received updated pickup times, but the car almost always arrived later than promised. It feels like the tracker is part of a deliberate deception to make you choose Uber over Lyft, to keep you from cancelling, to make you stand on the street early. The show contacted TurboTax and Uber; TurboTax did not respond, Uber did not arrange an interview but shared some data suggesting their pickup times are fairly accurate.

25:52 Field test: the pizza tracker is mostly real
Nick biked to a local Domino's to stake out, while Alex ordered a half-Hawaiian half-pepperoni pizza at home and monitored the tracker in real time. Nick ordered another pepperoni pizza in the store as cover. The tracker showed 'Ivan' making the pizza, but when Nick asked the employee's name, he said 'Alex.' The tracker also showed 'quality check,' but Nick saw no quality inspector. However, David explained that because Domino's uses conveyor ovens, bake time is nearly fixed, so the tracker automatically jumps to the next step after a set time. Eventually, the pizza came out, was boxed, and was driven away by Alex (aka Ivan), with Nick biking after, nearly mistaken for a stalker. Alex pressed 'delivered' at Nick's door, and the tracker updated quickly. Conclusion: the tracker is mostly accurate, but 'Ivan making' and 'quality check' are fake.

item.title: AI Proves in Half an Hour a Math Theorem Humans Couldn't Crack in a Year
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-instituteforad-ai-半小时证出人类一年没做出的数学定理/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-instituteforad-ai-半小时证出人类一年没做出的数学定理/
item.description: A stuck L^p problem, a five-page proof from AI in half an hour, a 60-page paper compressed to its core lemma, and the threshold for continuous density pushed from 588 down to 9.
item.content:encoded:
A stuck L^p problem, a five-page proof from AI in half an hour, a 60-page paper compressed to its core lemma, and the threshold for continuous density pushed from 588 down to 9.

If you care about what AI can actually do in pure mathematics, this episode gives a concrete, verifiable case: not assisted computation, but a proof structure humans hadn't thought of.

0:18 For the first time, AI had a good idea
The speaker says this is the first time he has encountered a model that "really had a good idea" on a problem he had worked on for a long time, and that this idea led to "very elegant efficient progress." Note his wording: it's not that AI helped him compute, it's that AI produced a proof approach he hadn't thought of. He credits the result to Astra and says it was done only last week.

8:13 The key theorem: absolute continuity automatically carries L^p
The core theorem is: if a self-similar measure μ is absolutely continuous, then its density automatically lies in some L^p with p greater than 1. What really excites the speaker is not the fact itself but that p is quantitative — p can be expressed explicitly in terms of the mass μ gives to small balls. Because p is quantitative, one can bring over methods for studying explicit absolute continuity, construct explicit L^p examples, and from there get continuous density.

12:27 p can never be made uniform
The speaker specifically warns: p can never be made uniform. For any dimension d and any p greater than 1, there exists some self-similar measure that lies in L^1 but not in L^p. So this quantitative result cannot be read as "all absolutely continuous self-similar measures have uniform L^p integrability" — it is a case-by-case bound that depends on the mass distribution.

23:45 Splitting λ into odd and even parts
The trick for proving continuous density: split the random series of the Bernoulli convolution into odd and even terms; after factoring out one λ from the odd part, what remains is exactly the even part. So μ_λ equals the convolution of μ_{λ²} with itself. If λ² falls in the range where Solomyak proved L^2 holds almost surely, then the convolution of two L^2 functions is continuous, and μ_λ has continuous density. This is the bridge from an L^2 result to continuity.

34:17 A 60-page paper compressed into 5 pages
The speaker says the core idea was actually one he and his collaborators already had, but AI was "extremely elegant and efficient" in using it. Varju's paper is 60 pages, and his own paper is also very long; AI compressed the passage from one result to another into 5 pages, and after "maybe a bit of a weakening," another 5 pages sufficed to get a stronger conclusion. He stresses this is not AI thinking up the core idea for him, but AI combining known tools in a way he "could have never" done.

36:18 Half an hour to run, 50 hours to formalise
Asked about runtime, the speaker says "not long, maybe half an hour." The whole result was then formalised in Lean, which took about 50 hours. He also mentions tricks like goal command that let the model "really try hard." The comparison: it might have taken him a year himself, and "if you sent me this paper to referee, I would like who is this person?"

39:21 The threshold for continuous density drops from 588 to 9
For the case λ = 1 - 1/n, AI proves μ_λ is continuous when n is greater than 588 — the speaker says this is not yet the result of him pushing the constant, "if I push the constant, I could easily push the constant more." Even more striking is another result: absolutely continuous when n is greater than 9, which the speaker says "I could not dare think I could prove"; he himself pushed for two and a half hours to get to 9, while the ideal target is 3.

43:23 The key lemma comes from an obscure paper
At the heart of the proof is a lemma from geometric measure theory: for an L^1 positive function f, if the mass of a set inside a small ball is small and the integral of f over that set is also small, then f lies in some explicit L^p, with p given explicitly by C, ε, and A. The speaker says this lemma is "not too difficult to prove," about a page, but "extremely difficult to find because it's not a very well-known fact" — it was dug out of some random papers.

item.title: Looney Tunes Animator: Characters Aren't Drawn, They're Thought Up
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freshair-乐一通-动画师-角色不是画出来的-是想出来的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freshair-乐一通-动画师-角色不是画出来的-是想出来的/
item.description: Chuck Jones said the key to animation isn't what a character looks like or how it's drawn, but "who he is" — he understood the character first, which let Daffy be cowardly and swaggering at once, and let Bugs Bunny strike back only after being provoked.
item.content:encoded:
Chuck Jones said the key to animation isn't what a character looks like or how it's drawn, but "who he is" — he understood the character first, which let Daffy be cowardly and swaggering at once, and let Bugs Bunny strike back only after being provoked.

The first half, the Chuck Jones interview, is information-dense; the second half, the Cassandra Wilson segment, is mostly music appreciation, so you can listen to just the interview portion.

0:00 Bugs Bunny's violence wouldn't pass review today
Comedian Dustin Nickerson tried showing classic cartoons to his young daughter and found they hadn't become harmless with time: many characters have speech impediments and behave aggressively. Pepe Le Pew forcibly holds a female character so she can't leave, while other characters murder each other — the coyote wants to kill the bird. This runs counter to the cartoon impression in viewers' memories that "everyone is friends."

4:04 A film shelved by Warner was saved by an independent distributor
After Coyote vs. Acme was finished, it was shelved by Warner Bros. Discovery and written off financially. This year an independent distributor bought the rights for $50 million, and last month it finally opened. The film screened in relatively few theaters across the U.S., but it has already recouped almost its entire cost domestically, with another $30 million overseas. The movie itself is about the coyote suing the Acme company, inspired by Ian Frazier's 1990 New Yorker parody article.

7:07 Daffy is cowardly and swaggering at the same time
Chuck Jones said Daffy is funny because he rushes in and fears to take a step at the same time, is both obsequious and domineering — like when we go into the boss's office to ask for a raise, swaggering at the door but obsequious once inside, and with Daffy both happen simultaneously. He admitted he couldn't understand "crazy" characters, so he always had to "pasteurize" a character and figure out who he is. He stressed that the point of character animation isn't what the character looks like, nor how it's drawn, but "who he is."

9:11 Bugs Bunny is a comedy hero, not a comedy loser
Jones first did Duck Amuck with Daffy, then later did Rabbit Rampage with Bugs Bunny, and the same setup didn't hold, because Bugs Bunny isn't that kind of character. He classified Bugs Bunny as a comedy hero, whereas the lineage of comedians like Chaplin and Buster Keaton are half-losers, more like ordinary people. He liked Daffy because Daffy keeps going forward, to the point where he himself would stop for fear of what others would think.

10:14 A two-hour "yes session" where no negative opinions were allowed
After 1946, Warner's cartoons were directed by three people: Fritz Freeling, Bob McKimpson and Jones. Whoever had an idea for a film would call the other directors and writers into a meeting they called a "yes session": for two hours no one was allowed to say anything negative, and if you had nothing to contribute you shut up. The result was that everyone participated in everyone else's films, but each director had absolute control over the content of his own films, and there was no infighting. Jones also admitted that if a good gag he'd given was used by Freeling and the audience laughed, he naturally wanted to go throw up — that's human nature, and it was the Daffy in him.

13:25 The narrower the rules, the better the comedy
Jones believed that in comedy, the more you narrow and restrict a character, the better it works: once Chaplin put on the Little Tramp outfit, what he could do was locked down. Once Roadrunner and Coyote were set in the American Southwest desert, the rules followed — Roadrunner must stay on the road, can never harm Coyote, and Coyote can only harm himself by buying those unlucky Acme products, and apart from "beep-beep" you hear no other sound in the whole film. Bugs Bunny is too strong and easily becomes a bully, so every film first lets him live his own life in his natural rabbit environment, until someone comes to take his skin or his life, and only then does he strike back.

16:30 Hiding one dirty frame in a twenty-fourth of a second
Jones admitted that Warner's animators all drew that kind of pornographic cartoon privately. He himself would sometimes slip a single frame — a twenty-fourth of a second — of a dirty image into a Pepe Le Pew film, then call the office manager over and say there seemed to be a little glitch here that he couldn't figure out. He knew no one could see it, but the manager would be shocked on the spot. He always kept a replacement frame on hand just in case, but he enjoyed doing it, in his words, to "reduce him to moccasins."

17:31 The networks cut films until they were incomprehensible
Jones said his scenes and lines were never censored; that was left to the "brilliant people" at the networks, and what they cut made the whole film incomprehensible. Both CBS and ABC did it. He found it absurd that the Roadrunner series, which drew the most complaints about violence, actually had no violence — Roadrunner never harmed Coyote, and Coyote was simply the victim of his own incompetence.

item.description: In 2025, fewer than 1% of IMO contestants scored full marks on Problem 6, and every AI got stuck on it. item.content:encoded:
In 2025, fewer than 1% of IMO contestants scored full marks on Problem 6, and every AI got stuck on it. What makes it hard isn't computation — it's that you have to understand first, have taste first, and only then start writing. And that is exactly what reinforcement learning struggles most to train.

The bulk of this episode is a complete walkthrough of one math problem, not AI industry analysis. Only the last 5 minutes discuss the relationship between AI and math, but those 5 minutes are worth hearing.

0:00 What blocks AI isn't computation, it's patience
On 2025 IMO Problem 6, fewer than 1% of the world's 600-plus top contestants scored full marks. By 2025, models from several institutions could answer every other problem correctly, and got stuck only on this one. DeepMind research director Thang Luong's explanation: the model has no patience — it won't spend time understanding the problem or developing a feel for it, it just starts solving. Karpathy adds a second reason: the model has no sense of what makes a problem or a strategy beautiful, and this problem's solution depends precisely on aesthetic judgment.

6:11 Genius is really the residue of experience
Facing this problem, the most obvious construction is to put all the X's on the diagonal and cover the remaining region with horizontal tiles, giving 2(n-1) tiles. But that construction is too obvious to be the answer IMO wants. Karpathy inserts a seemingly unrelated cube-cutting brainteaser here: a 3x3x3 cube cut into 27 small cubes, where you're allowed to rearrange the pieces after each cut — what's the minimum number of cuts? The answer is 6, because each of the 6 faces of the very center cube needs its own separate cut. That proof idea — fix your attention on one face of the internal structure — is exactly the key to the tiling problem later.

12:17 The most efficient tiling has every tile touching four X's
Highlight all four edges of every X, and each time you place a tile, switch off the edges it touches. In an inefficient tiling, a tile touches only 1 or even 0 X's; in an efficient tiling, every tile touches 4 X's. This yields a conjecture: the optimal tiling should make as many tiles as possible touch 4 distinct X's. But look further: an X cannot sit in the middle of a tile's edge — that would make the two tiles above and below conflict on the left, since a column can't contain two X's. The X must sit at a corner of the tiles, with four tiles pinwheeling around it. With square tiles of side length k, you can tile a large grid of side length k². And 2025 happens to be 45², a coincidence that makes the construction look extremely promising.

19:27 Highlight only one direction and the proof misses the tiles on one side
Highlight the edges of all X's: 4k² edges total, each tile touches at most 4, subtract the 4 boundary edges that don't need to be touched, and you get the lower bound k²-1. But the target lower bound is k²+2k-3, off by a term proportional to k. The problem is that you only highlighted the right edge: the correspondence you get this way is tight on the right side of the diagram, but misses a large number of tiles concentrated on the left. Switching to any other single direction is the same — the missed tiles always cluster on one side. Karpathy says math rewards you for respecting symmetry and punishes you for not respecting it — pick an arbitrary direction, and the weakness shows up in the inequality.

27:38 Cut the grid into four regions, highlight each edge only once
The solution is to draw two paths: one going up-right along the X's, one going down-right, dividing the whole diagram into four regions. If an X is in the right region, highlight its right edge; if in the top region, highlight its top edge — left, right, top, bottom each handle one region. X's lying on the boundary get two edges highlighted. This both recovers the missing highlighted edges and guarantees each tile touches at most one highlighted edge — because when a tile sits in the left region, the X above it cannot have its bottom edge highlighted, the X below it cannot have its top edge highlighted, and the X to its left cannot have its right edge highlighted. This diagram is the core of the entire proof.

31:48 The problem reduces to a pure permutation problem
Label each X with the row it sits in; since each row contains exactly one X, these labels form a permutation of 1 to k². The up-right path corresponds to an increasing subsequence, the down-right path to a decreasing subsequence. Let LIS be the length of the longest increasing subsequence and LDS the longest decreasing subsequence; the total number of highlighted edges is k² + LIS + LDS - 4 (plus 1 more when the two paths intersect, making it -3). To prove the target lower bound k²+2k-3, it suffices to prove LIS + LDS ≥ 2k, that is, that the average of the two is at least k. At this point the grid has completely vanished, and what remains is a pure fact about permutations.

39:59 The proof of Erdős-Szekeres is itself a gem
This pure permutation fact is the Erdős-Szekeres theorem: in any permutation, the product of the lengths of the longest increasing subsequence and the longest decreasing subsequence is at least the length n of the permutation. An IMO contestant could just cite the theorem and finish, but Karpathy chooses to give the proof too. The method is to label each position with a pair of numbers: the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending there, and the length of the longest decreasing subsequence ending there. Because the numbers in a permutation are all distinct, the two label pairs at any two positions must differ — if the later number is larger, the first label increases by at least one; if smaller, the second label increases by at least one. Plot these label pairs as coordinate points: the longest increasing subsequence is the width of the bounding box, the longest decreasing subsequence is the height, and width times height equals the number of lattice points, which is the length of the permutation.

48:08 Beyond the proof there's another layer: making the proof feel obvious
Karpathy says knowing a proof is only a very small part of deeply understanding mathematics. When he and Nishad Dulkhar made this video, their first reaction to reading the original proof was "I know it's true, but how would anyone come up with this." What they wanted to contribute wasn't a new proof but a narrative, so that when viewers reach the proof it no longer feels like it appeared out of nowhere. He has a name for this: motivated explanation. This bears directly on AI and math: if a machine can generate proofs but doesn't bring human understanding, then it's completely meaningless. And academia has long used "proof" as a proxy metric for progress, which exposes an urgent need — for a new, independent way to measure whether a publication actually advances human understanding.

item.title: NASA Administrator: We Are Not a Procurement Agency, We Are a Nuclear-Powered NASA
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-nasa-局长-我们不是采购机构-是核动力-nasa/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-nasa-局长-我们不是采购机构-是核动力-nasa/
item.description: Jared Isaacman says NASA used to spread resources across every congressional district and partner for partnership's sake, and the result is a lunar rocket less efficient than the Saturn V; what he wants to build is nuclear power and nuclear propulsion, and hand low Earth orbit to companies like SpaceX.
item.content:encoded:
Jared Isaacman says NASA used to spread resources across every congressional district and partner for partnership's sake, and the result is a lunar rocket less efficient than the Saturn V; what he wants to build is nuclear power and nuclear propulsion, and hand low Earth orbit to companies like SpaceX.

This is the policy manifesto of NASA's new administrator, with information density concentrated on the lunar south pole, nuclear power and the Mars plan, though the back half of the interview is soft and the Q&A quality is middling.

2:06 NASA used to spread resources thin to please everyone
Isaacman divides NASA's problems into two kinds: externally imposed and self-inflicted. Partnering for partnership's sake turned partnerships into a drag on missions rather than an accelerator. The result is that Orion cannot inject into low lunar orbit the way Apollo did; the previous administration cancelled Mars Sample Return because the cost would exceed an aircraft carrier. He also says NASA built programs that are "too big to fail and too expensive to ever really succeed," counting on them to survive across administrations. Core capabilities were rented out, outsourced or simply lost, and progress that should have taken months turned into years at greatly increased cost.

3:07 The lunar rocket is less efficient than the Saturn V from sixty years ago
He offers a jarring comparison: China's rockets were designed when locomotives still burned coal, and today China operates 25,000 miles of high-speed rail and is only a few years from its own Apollo 11 moment. Meanwhile NASA's lunar rocket is less efficient than the Saturn V at converting launch mass into payload headed to the Moon; the gap between Artemis 1 and Artemis 2 is longer than all 12 Gemini missions of sixty years ago combined. The lunar space station puts astronauts in a position to look down on the most coveted lunar real estate, rather than working on the surface and occupying it.

7:07 The lunar south pole has only a few good parking spots
The Moon's surface area is roughly that of Africa, but the south pole is only about the size of Washington, D.C., and the usable permanently shadowed craters are limited. Those craters hold water ice, and the environment is harsher than Mars itself; the crater walls can also provide near-permanent solar illumination. So good landing sites are very few. He notes that a Starship-sized vehicle landing on the lunar surface will blast out a crater and throw debris, further shrinking the usable spots. China's robotic mission is targeting Shackleton Crater next year, and China and Russia are also cooperating on a nuclear-powered lunar base.

8:07 Launching a 100-kilowatt fission reactor in 2028
NASA is saying goodbye to failed nuclear programs that have not left the lab since 1965, and in 2028 will launch SR1 Freedom, a 100-kilowatt fission reactor. The mission will fly past Mars and release Skyfall, carrying three Ingenuity-class helicopters, using ground-penetrating radar to scout subsurface ice and future landing sites. He calls this the beginning of a "nuclear-powered NASA," turning its workforce and facilities back to missions that are nearly impossible and have no obvious commercial case. SR2, SR3 and SR4 will follow, with targets including Enceladus, Europa and Titan, moons with oceans and complex chemistry.

23:22 The hardest part of Mars is not getting there, it is coming back
Pure chemical propulsion can also send astronauts to Mars, at a speed comparable to going to the Moon, and the habitation problem was solved long ago. The hard part is how to come back: you need to manufacture propellant on the Martian surface, and the plan is robots plus football-field-sized solar arrays, which also have to be regularly dusted off after sandstorms. He says doing this at one atmosphere and 1G on Earth is already extremely difficult. NASA's answer is to stop doing what industry already does well and turn to next-generation capabilities with no commercial case: fission power, plus a chemically boosted nuclear transfer vehicle using krypton or xenon rather than manufacturing propellant on the Martian surface.

25:23 Hiring is not hard, retaining talent is
NASA's internship program accepts only 1% of applicants, so there is no recruiting problem early on. The problem is whether it can keep people. If NASA does the same things as SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Stoke and ULA while still using fifty-year-old space shuttle hardware, it will lose talent. His approach: once a breakthrough has a commercial case, such as launch, NASA becomes one of many customers, hands the capability to industry and turns to the next new thing. SR1 is only the beginning of the nuclear-powered NASA, their Nautilus, and a whole nuclear fleet will follow.

27:24 Nuclear propulsion is essentially an ion thruster in space
He explains the principle: the ion thrusters on Starlink satellites use solar power to ionize and accelerate krypton or xenon and expel it, giving extremely high exhaust velocity, very low thrust but very high efficiency, so propellant lasts a long time. The farther you get from the Sun, the more useless solar power becomes, and near Jupiter it is essentially negligible. At that point you switch to the heat of a nuclear reactor, starting at 100 kilowatts and possibly scaling to 250 kilowatts or even megawatts. The reactor should run as hot as possible, using high-temperature materials and a closed Brayton cycle to convert heat to electricity, then drive the same thrusters, just scaled up from 12, 14, 25 kilowatts.

28:24 NASA does not lack budget, it lacks capital allocation ability
He says NASA does not have a top line problem, but has long been terrible at capital allocation, partly by NASA's own choice and partly imposed by others. The budget is now $25 billion. He asks how many founders are in the room, and says $25 billion is a lot of money and can build rather amazing hardware. In aeronautics, he complains that NASA's aeronautics budget is used to subsidize high-TRL programs at big contractors, such as a forty-year-old engine where NASA is asked to pay to squeeze out another 3% in fuel efficiency. He wants to return to radical airframe and engine designs.

item.title: Wanting to Save the World Is No Excuse for a Monopoly Agreement
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-moneystuff-想拯救世界-不是搞垄断协议的借口/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-moneystuff-想拯救世界-不是搞垄断协议的借口/
item.description: AI labs want to jointly slow down model development, but four giants sitting down to talk about deceleration is, legally, a textbook antitrust conspiracy — wanting to save the world is not a defense.
item.content:encoded:
AI labs want to jointly slow down model development, but four giants sitting down to talk about deceleration is, legally, a textbook antitrust conspiracy — wanting to save the world is not a defense.

Three segments: the insider-trading evidence problem, Dario's deceleration memo, and pension privatization. Medium information density; the last two segments are worth more.

2:05 Suing a hundred John Does doesn't fly with the judge
Susquehanna spotted someone buying large amounts of short-dated put options in Chinese brokerage stocks before cross-border trading was restricted, so it sued 100 John Does to freeze the accounts. But the judge denied the preliminary injunction: it could not be proven that all 100 of these people were conspiring to trade on inside information. Levine's breakdown is that only a tiny few may have actually gotten inside information, while the rest just saw the tape move and piled in — and piling into a publicly visible move is itself entirely legal. The ones who can actually figure out who is who are the securities regulators, not the market makers who got picked off.

8:13 The market maker may not have lost that much
Susquehanna claims it lost about $70 million on these puts, but Levine points out that this is only half the story: as an options market maker, after selling puts it would usually hedge immediately, possibly by shorting the stock, or by buying puts back from another client or another market maker. If Citadel Securities and Susquehanna were both selling and both buying that day, they were effectively betting against each other and should in theory be suing each other. So the "lost $70 million" figure obscures the fact that they were also hedging, and may even have been net up on the day.

15:21 Not training new models is actually more profitable
Levine offers a counterintuitive business logic: model capability is now ahead of deployment in many domains, and Anthropic and OpenAI are working with private equity firms to spread AI through enterprises. If they stopped model development for a year, they could make a lot of money selling existing models, with quite good unit economics. But competitive pressure forces every frontier lab to keep burning huge sums training the next model — both to win customers on the leaderboards and to win researchers, because researchers want to go to the best lab. So "slowing down" is good for business, but no one dares unilaterally lay down their weapons.

19:25 Four of them sitting down to talk deceleration is collusion
Since no one dares slow down unilaterally, could the four frontier labs sit down and reach an agreement? Levine says this is legally a classic antitrust conspiracy — like the case in which BlackRock was sued by several state attorneys general: ESG investors got coal companies to produce less coal on the grounds that global warming is bad for humanity, but the effect was higher coal prices, making them the OPEC of coal. The line in the ruling is "wanting to save the world is no excuse for an antitrust conspiracy." Dario's memo also added a footnote saying antitrust law would need to be appropriately amended before they would be allowed to sit in a room and discuss shutting down killer robots.

22:28 The founding documents are all handwritten by humans
Sylvia read Kevin Roos's book on the AGI race (out October 6; she had a pre-read copy) and found a contrast: every dramatic turning point in the book corresponds to a human handwritten memo — Dario's Pacing the Frontier, the Say AGI memo, and so on. And yet what everyone discusses now is "was this written by AI." Reading Dario's memo, she instinctively wondered "was this written by Claude," and concluded it did not read like AI at all — these people are philosophers, writing original founding texts. But the next generation will probably just ask Claude what to do.

27:31 A 401k has no funding gap, only a balance that's too small
A pension is a future cash flow a company has promised, and the company must invest to match that liability; invest wrong and you get a funding gap, which is why ERISA steps in to regulate pension insolvency. A 401k is not a promised cash flow, just a pool of money: if stocks fall, they fall, and there is no such thing as a "billion-dollar funding gap" on the books, only "the number in your account is lower than you want." This eliminates concentration risk — with a 401k, pension insolvency can never happen. The cost is that risk shifts from the company to the individual.

30:37 Pensions were actually great clients for Wall Street
The popular story is that the shift from pensions to 401ks was good for Wall Street, because it turned people who would have retired on a pension into retail clients trading their own accounts. Levine pushes back: a pension is itself an excellent client for Wall Street, because its time horizon is long and it can make the spicy investments retail investors won't touch — private equity, private credit. The 401k, over these decades, became cheap index funds, and retail investors actually pay extremely low fees. So now the financial industry is pushing to "revive the pension," stuffing private assets into retirement accounts, because you can't make any money charging one basis point on a public stock index.

32:44 Retail says long-term, but its hands want liquidity
Private credit BDCs raise money from retail investors on the logic that "you have a 30-year horizon, you don't need liquidity, you should take the liquidity premium." Then this year software companies delivered bad news, investors rushed to redeem, and the BDCs could only say that each quarter only 5% of people would be allowed to redeem. Levine calls this a "psychological liquidity mismatch": the fund really is making long-term investments and really should not sell long-term assets to meet redemptions; but retail investors psychologically want more liquidity than the fund offers. In theory, selling private assets to retirement savers is right; in practice, it's hard.

item.title: Hard Tech Is Now a Fifth of YC Batches: Software Companies Are Being Eaten by Agents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ycsp-硬科技占-yc-批次两成-软件公司正在被智能体吃掉/
