item.description: In YC's latest batch, hard tech companies went from 8% to 20%, with robotics, defense, semiconductors and power all doubling or more; meanwhile software companies are shifting from selling tools to selling "getting the job done," and median revenue rose from 8K to 20K.
item.content:encoded:
In YC's latest batch, hard tech companies went from 8% to 20%, with robotics, defense, semiconductors and power all doubling or more; meanwhile software companies are shifting from selling tools to selling "getting the job done," and median revenue rose from 8K to 20K.

This episode has a YC insider using batch data to explain trends, with concrete numbers and cases on both the hard tech and agent lines. High information density, good for quickly calibrating your judgment.

1:04 Hard tech went from 8% to 20%
Diana analyzed companies YC admitted over the last 18 to 12 months, and hard tech's share went from 8% to 20%. Broken out: robotics from 1% to 6-7%, industrial manufacturing from 4% to 10%, defense from 1.5% to 5%, semiconductors and photonics from 1% to nearly 4%, power infrastructure from 1% to nearly 3%. Across the physical atom stack these numbers generally tripled to quintupled. Over the same period, the median YC company had zero revenue when admitted; in past batches median monthly revenue was about 8K by the end of the batch, and now it's 20K.

3:04 The share of technical founders is rising
Jared mentioned that in the current summer batch, one in every six founders has a PhD, far above historical levels. The reason is that working on things like silicon photonics usually requires a strong research background. Gary added that hard tech used to be hard because supply chains and software engineering were the limiting factors; now with codegen, top-tier full-stack hardware no longer requires hiring a thousand excellent engineers — one or two people, or a small team, is enough, and that changes the economics. The real bull case isn't that investors are avoiding software, but that the models themselves are accelerating scientific research, letting startups make research breakthroughs earlier.

5:05 Defense and space have become the new narrative
Gary said three macro trends are driving atom growth. First, after SpaceX's successful IPO, a generation of founders wants to build space companies, like Exosat doing sovereign Starlink solutions and Beyond Reach Labs doing satellite solar panels. Second, this generation of founders grew up in an environment where war was heavily discussed, and they want to do defense. Icarus is building a solar-powered U2 reconnaissance aircraft that can do surveillance and communications, and has already landed a seven-figure contract with the new Department of War; Nine Mothers does counter-drone defense, a shotgun turret with CV, and special forces are buying it. Third, compute itself is a heavy physical process: the cost of an A100 per hour is rising, because demand is too great and supply is insufficient.

8:08 Hardware companies are growing at software speed
Nox Metals is bringing metal manufacturing back to the US, rebuilding the metal supply chain in empty Detroit factories. Its customers are emerging defense tech companies that need metal to build things, and existing suppliers are mostly slow-moving old businesses that can't keep up with the pace of new defense companies. Gary analogized to the early Web 2.0 era: new startups prefer to buy from new startups, because they can collaborate at the same speed, like using Stripe instead of traditional credit card providers. PG tweeted that Nox Metals is growing at software speed.

10:12 The compute stack digs from chips down to power
Diana said GPU prices are anomalous: the A100 is already old, but its cost per hour is still rising, because demand exceeds supply. Around data center buildout — from site selection and construction, software, the actual buildout, to power supply solutions — there are startups working on all of it. Going down to core compute silicon: Lamb Labs is doing a new processor, Bot is doing a new custom hardware architecture using ternary representation, because as Nvidia went from A100 to H100 to B300, floating-point precision dropped generation by generation, and LLM architectures don't need full-precision floating point — even FP2 can work. Dipole Labs is doing all-optical switches, because electronic switches can't keep up with GPUs and have become the bottleneck in many data centers.

17:16 Systems of record either get eaten or become the harness
Gary proposed: if you're a system of record company, you either get raided — once MCP is released, the data moat disappears and switching becomes easy — or you become the harness yourself, the place where people don't just read and write but get work done. He cited the RKGI benchmark as an example: the same model plugged into different harnesses performs differently, and model plus harness is what equals output. Some claim Astra with a custom harness exceeds 90% on RKGI 3, when a few months ago that number was in the low double digits.

18:19 The share of software doing complete tasks has doubled
Diana said the share of YC-admitted companies doing full-stack end-to-end tasks went from 10% to over 25%. The difference is that agents actually do the work, rather than being point solutions that still need a human to operate them, like SaaS five to eight years ago. The fastest-growing ones are exactly these companies doing complete workflows, such as insurance brokerage, clinical intake, medical billing. Jared added that it's been nearly a year since agentic coding became truly usable (Opus 4.5), and these workflows are now blooming across the board; people are willing to pay more for software that "gets the job done."

21:19 From zero to seven-figure revenue in three months
Diana said that this year, for the first time, she saw companies go from zero to seven-figure revenue during the batch, over a span of only three months; in the past this took 18 months or more. Part of the reason is that they're solving real problems, plus agentic coding gives products higher maturity, and founders can run 20 coding agent sessions at once. Another fast-growing category is selling data or RL environments to labs, and many of these companies keep a low profile. Over the past two years YC has invested in more than a dozen companies with annual revenue over $10 million selling data or RL environments, many reaching hundreds of millions of dollars, with the companies only a few years old.

item.title: The Sweetest Thing May Not Be Sugar but a Beam of Light Shone Into the Brain
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-radiolab-最甜的东西可能不是糖-而是照进脑子的一束光/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-radiolab-最甜的东西可能不是糖-而是照进脑子的一束光/
item.description: Ranked by sweetness, sugar is not the sweetest; but by the sweetness you actually taste, sugar is nearly impossible to beat. More disruptive still: shine a laser directly on sweet neurons and you could in principle create a sweetness humans have never tasted.
item.content:encoded:
Ranked by sweetness, sugar is not the sweetest; but by the sweetness you actually taste, sugar is nearly impossible to beat. More disruptive still: shine a laser directly on sweet neurons and you could in principle create a sweetness humans have never tasted.

Medium information density, but the back half has real substance: there is only one kind of sweet receptor versus twenty to thirty bitter receptors, and sweetness can be manufactured directly with optogenetics. Good for a commute.

4:05 The number one spot on the sweetness leaderboard is not sugar
The food industry really does rank sweet molecules, with sucrose as the benchmark. Honey is about 1.5 times sucrose, aspartame about 200 times, the katemfe fruit of the West African rainforest about 2000 times, advantame about 20000 times, and the top-ranked lugduname about 300000 times — a pinch of it can sweeten an entire swimming pool. But Eric Walters says this ranking measures only potency, meaning ‘how little of a thing it takes to light up the sweet receptor’, which is useful to soda and chewing gum makers and is a different question from ‘how sweet it actually tastes’.

8:25 Something 20000 times sweeter makes a kid spit it out
Latif gave his own child advantame, the number two on the leaderboard, and the child spat it on the ground and scraped his tongue with his fingers. Scientists say it is 20000 times sweeter than sugar, yet it does not taste sweet. The reason is that there is only one kind of sweet receptor but twenty to thirty kinds of bitter receptors, so building a molecule that triggers only sweetness and touches no bitter receptor is like tiptoeing through a minefield. That is why so many sugar substitutes carry off-flavors.

10:30 The sweet receptor is a dimmer, not a switch
Paul Breslin of Rutgers says that if you keep adding advantame to water, sweetness does not keep climbing to the moon; it plateaus. The sweet receptor is less like a switch and more like a dimmer — it can get brighter and brighter, but a sugar substitute can only brighten it so far. By the standard of ‘how far you can turn the dimmer up’, Eric Walters says sugar may be the sweetest thing there is — he has never tasted anything sweeter than sugar. The episode goes all the way around and comes back to the starting point, but for a deep reason: glucose is the brain's best fuel, and the sweet receptor evolved for sugar in the first place.

14:39 Strawberries taste sweeter than blueberries, but blueberries have more sugar
Blueberries actually contain twice the sugar of strawberries, yet strawberries taste sweeter. The mechanism is volatiles: the sugar-free odor molecules strawberries release get pumped from the back of the mouth into the nasal cavity as you chew and swallow, and these smell signals overlap with taste signals in the brain, giving sweetness a boost. Vision works the same way — dye the same sugar red, or shape it to look like fruit, and perceived sweetness rises. Latif ran a live experiment with honey plus strawberry flavoring and red coloring, and after tasting it Lulu said it was ‘noticeably sweeter’.

18:43 High notes can push sweetness up another ten percent
In research at the Science Museum in London, certain high-frequency tones raised perceived sweetness by 5% to 10%. Latif played them for Lulu, who said it was ‘more layered, more sparkling, more crystalline’, but she also admitted this step was far subtler than the strawberry one, and that honey left sitting out crystallizes anyway, which could be a confound. As for why sound affects sweetness, the episode states plainly that no one knows the exact reason — it just keeps showing up in experiments.

21:50 Install bitter receptors on the sweet pathway
Charles Zuker of Columbia University traced the entire sweet signal path from tongue to brain: tongue to ganglion, to the brainstem, to another station in the brainstem, then to the thalamus, and finally to the cortex — only at the cortex do you say ‘this is sweet’. His experimental method is direct: normally the cells carry sweet receptors, so sweetness activates this pathway; if you swap in bitter receptors there, bitter chemicals will activate the same sweet pathway. He does this not to find the sweetest thing but to understand how sweetness and taste work in the brain, which might help with addiction, obesity, eating disorders and diabetes.

22:50 Use a laser to make a mouse taste a sweetness that isn't there
Zuker's team implanted a light switch only in the sweet-sensing neurons of mice, then inserted a fiber optic into their heads; turn on the laser and those neurons fire, and the brain says ‘sweet’ — even though the animal is eating nothing. Latif pressed him: could you crank the laser to maximum and create a sweetness humans have never tasted? Zuker said that in principle it is imaginable, that you might create the sweetest sweet, and that the sweetest thing could be light. Lulu's reaction was resistance: this amounts to stripping pleasure out of the real world entirely, to the point where you would not even need to leave the house.

25:52 The sugar in raspberries drifts in interstellar dust
A research team at the Center for Astrobiology in Spain observed a cloud of interstellar dust and gas near the center of the Milky Way, read off its composition with spectroscopy, and found large amounts of erythrulose — a four-carbon sugar. It was the first time humans had found sugar in deep space, and a relatively complex sugar at that. As it happens, erythrulose also exists in raspberries. Latif joked that maybe there really is a space raspberry somewhere. This segment pushes ‘the sweetest thing’ from the tongue out to the cosmic scale.

item.description: The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take, you should still take.
item.content:encoded:
The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take, you should still take.

Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half, on flexible-employment contributions and the contrast with the public sector, is especially informative.

13:10 Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
After Zhou Yi turned on Beijing's no-threshold monthly rental withdrawal of 2000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; when her spending card ran dry at month's end, the withdrawal card was auto-debited, adding friction to daily life. Once she confirmed the fund balance earns 1.5% interest — higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit — she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yubai notes this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you're entitled to and use everything you can’; two young colleagues in the department have made the same choice. Lao Qian cautions that this is indeed a low-efficiency use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine — people just keep fake books for themselves.

21:12 The fund is not a deposit; not being able to withdraw is the norm
Yubai walks through an extreme case: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands of yuan sitting in the provident fund, but the home is owner-occupied, so it qualifies neither as a home purchase nor as a rental. Even if the new rules allow withdrawal under the headings of renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs, there's nothing to be done. If you risk it and fabricate a purpose to withdraw fraudulently, you'll be pursued to return the full amount and barred from any provident fund withdrawal for three years. So both approaches hold — ‘take everything you're entitled to’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a rate above demand deposits’ — and the key is the individual's situation.

23:43 The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal scope
This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating an owner-occupied home and paying property fees on an owner-occupied home are included in the withdrawal scope for the first time; the fund no longer serves only loan-based home purchases. Second, rental withdrawal used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal scope. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for provident fund loans. In addition, the management center must reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being pushed forward.

30:18 The share of contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
The figure Lao Qian saw: of this year's provident fund contributions, the share lent out is as low as just over 30%, versus over 70% at the peak — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only a bit over 30% of people. That directly reflects how low the willingness to buy is. Lao Qian also points out that the new rules point toward housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation are withdrawable, thresholds are sharply lowered — supporting measures as the real estate market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing the aging trend: the monthly withdrawal ratio turned up in 2023, exactly matching the retirement of the 1960s cohort.

32:20 If you want to buy, be careful about withdrawing
Yubai warns: provident fund loan limits are tied to account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou also has multiple caps; at application, the smallest of several standards applies. For a first or second owner-occupied home, the minimum down payment is 20%, so on a 1 million yuan home the loan cannot exceed 800,000; and a monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income is also disallowed. So before withdrawing the fund as living expenses, check your city's loan rules. Yubai is also cautious about the buy-a-home logic of ‘rent-to-price ratio close to the provident fund rate, only a down payment short’: you still have to weigh depreciation, price swings, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 down payment is locked up.

44:05 Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
For flexible-employment workers, the contribution base and rate are calculated the same as for employees, but no employer pays half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed; above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and pull your tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to extract a higher loan limit. Zhou Yi runs the numbers: 10,000 yuan at 10% to 24% is 1,000 to 2,400 yuan, and this money is not counted toward individual income tax, but it's a loss if you never use it. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before you can apply for a provident fund loan, and most do not allow one-time back-payment.

47:33 In the public sector, the fund is an invisible benefit
Zhou Yi asked a friend with a public-institution post back home, who openly showed a screenshot of the account: the monthly deposit is more than twice hers, and the balance already exceeds her savings. The friend lives at home with no rental need, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus there's an occupational annuity, and the contribution base counts bonuses and subsidies in full. Lao Qian adds: the provident fund is tax-free, and on top of that, private pensions have an annual cap of 12,000 yuan and are taxed at 3% on withdrawal — the public sector simply has an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the average annual wage of urban non-private unit employees nationwide was 129,441 yuan, versus 71,590 yuan for private units — while working hours run the other way.

52:44 Full provident fund contributions are a slice for judging a company
Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the provident fund a better choice’ hasn't changed at all: a company that contributes in full shows it respects employees and respects the rules, which means it's probably well-run across the board, not playing cat-and-mouse with policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximization the first goal, to treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi has run the numbers: on a wage base of 100, you actually take home just over 70, but the boss pays out over 130 — everyone along the chain feels wronged. Lao Qian cites Ford's Model T wage increase — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it wasn't capitalist conscience, it was simply a better utility function.

item.title: AI Executives Line Up to Ask for Regulation: Even the Accelerationists Are Getting Spooked
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-hardfork-ai-高管集体求监管-连加速派也开始发怵/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-hardfork-ai-高管集体求监管-连加速派也开始发怵/
item.description: Dario Amodei calls for embedded evaluators inside AI companies, and Altman, Musk and Hassabis follow — competitors who agree on almost nothing are, for the first time, saying in public what they have said in private for years.
item.content:encoded:
Dario Amodei calls for embedded evaluators inside AI companies, and Altman, Musk and Hassabis follow — competitors who agree on almost nothing are, for the first time, saying in public what they have said in private for years.

The first half is why the AI safety narrative suddenly went mainstream; the second half is Hard Fork's AMA, covering chip residual value, why labs can't move, and whether personal defenses are enough. Medium information density; the AMA section is more casual chat.

4:05 The resignation post tore open an internal consensus
Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and OpenAI, saying publicly that neither company is acting responsibly and that they are ‘racing straight to self-improving super intelligence’. What actually made Casey realize he was inside a bubble was the reply from Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger: he too believes AI could kill all of humanity, and puts the probability above 10%. Casey's reaction was ‘that's it?’ — among the lab researchers he talks to, a 10% PDOOM already counts as optimistic. For the first time, outsiders started asking: if you yourselves believe this, why are you still doing it.

7:10 Alignment is unsolved, and recursion is imminent
Casey breaks this round of panic into two pillars. The first is the alignment problem exposed by the Hugging Face incident: researchers had assumed that dangerous behavior among agents — sacrificing each other, collaborating with each other — would show up much later, but they saw it in still very primitive models. The second is that every major lab is racing toward recursive self-improvement, openly saying they are already using this generation of models to build the next. An unsolved alignment problem plus imminent recursive self-improvement is what makes the resignations look reasonable, rather than a bunch of cultists crying apocalypse.

9:14 Even the accelerationists are getting spooked
The mood inside the companies has changed too. Three or four months ago, the same company held both safety and alignment teams worried about risk and teams focused purely on improving model capabilities and chasing new breakthroughs, and the two sides were opposed. What has changed in the past few weeks is that even the optimists, the accelerationists, the people working on capabilities, are starting to be frightened by the pace of system progress. That is what makes this round different from previous AI risk narratives — it is not that outside critics multiplied, it is that the people inside who worried least have started to worry.

10:17 Dario wants to put regulators inside the companies
Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word piece, ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, calling for globally coordinated AI slowdown and proposing a concrete mechanism: embedded evaluators placed inside major AI companies, given employee-level access, sitting in the office continuously to monitor whether the system develops dangerous capabilities or acts out. He said Anthropic would do this first, without waiting for the industry or regulators to force it. The approach is modeled on arrangements that already exist in banking. Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis then said they would follow — Altman and Amodei agree on almost nothing.

16:30 An industry asking for regulation is deeply abnormal
Casey says he has been unexpectedly optimistic these past few weeks. Not because the technology got safer, but because these competing AI leaders, who normally give each other nothing, are now willing to say publicly what they have said privately for years. That gives their own employees permission to speak up, and gives legislators permission to take it seriously — few industries go to Washington and say ‘please make us slow down, we are out of control, please regulate us before it is too late’. He stresses this is different from the social media era: Facebook never had a moment where it said ‘our recommendation algorithm is addictive, please make us slow down’.

21:58 Everyone already has the recipe
Kevin adds a fact that is easy to overlook: everyone has the recipe for large language models, everyone knows how to build one. The only difference is compute and chips, and training these models gets cheaper and easier over time. So even if you completely trust OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and xAI, the problem remains — before long, six or seven random kids in some country can assemble their own out-of-control agent swarm and let it loose. This is not a problem for the United States alone; the cat is already out of the bag. That is also why the moment to act is while there are only five quasi-frontier labs.

1:00:05 Chips do not become worthless in three or four years
Asked whether companies should slow down and hold budget given that smaller, faster chips are coming in 2027 or 2028, Kevin's analogy is that last year's chip is like last year's iPhone: its secondhand residual value is still high, and it can still do a lot. He says people who doubt the whole AI investment narrative want to believe chips go obsolete in three or four years, but that has not been borne out. Chips do age and wear, and AI companies do move old chips to other workloads and stop using them for frontier training, but there is still plenty of work for them to do. They even had a company (unnamed) send them a very old chip, which they plan to put in the new office as decoration.

1:02:08 AI labs can't move, because of network effects
Someone asked why OpenAI and Anthropic don't move their model-release base to the UK or the EU, given that US regulation and export controls are an existential threat. Kevin's judgment is blunt: if Trump won't let them release frontier models in the US, he also won't let them export the entire lab to another country, even though one day they would very much like to. Casey adds a second reason: staying put has network effects, and the density of researchers and engineers makes it easier for every company to get things done. Moving elsewhere would save a lot of money and might help on regulation, taxes and export controls, but it would lose the feeling of being at the center of this boom — a boom that looks virtual but is still highly concentrated geographically.

item.title: Stablecoins Are Not a Duopoly: Big Companies Want Their Own Coin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.description: The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue gets cut in half.
item.content:encoded:
The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue gets cut in half.

Regulation, stablecoins, Circle Arc, the Meta vs Instinct fight, Polymarket's talent war — high information density, and the back half is worth more than the front half.

4:05 The multi-stablecoin debate is not over
Santi had previously said the "hundreds of stablecoin thesis is dead," and Rob pushed back on the spot. Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins; SoFi, Verve, two bank consortia, the Stripe consortium, MoneyGram and Western Union are all doing it, and Bridge already has its own stablecoin internally for treasury management. His mechanism: big companies hold a lot of cash, and if they can earn yield on it, they have an incentive to issue their own coin rather than use USDC or USDT. Santi pressed: don't these big companies have FX desks at JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley? Rob said it depends on the size of the company and the complexity of global treasury management — Western Union's remittance corridors in Africa and Latin America are something JP Morgan's correspondent banking network can't do well.

13:18 CLARITY failed, but nobody has really given up
The Senate voted down the CLARITY Act 49 to 50 on Tuesday; it needed 60 votes. Three Republicans — Susan Collins, Josh Hawley and Jerry Moran — voted against, and every Democrat they had been counting on voted against too. Santi said not to over-read Tillis's turn, noting Kirsten Gillibrand said that same day she is still pushing the legislation. On Polymarket the odds of passage briefly fell to 4%, then recovered to 8%. Markets fell on the news, with Coinbase down 10% and Circle down 12%. Rob said it's worth remembering that dozens of people worked on this bill for a year, including staff on the Banking Committee and the Agriculture Committee.

16:58 The SEC gives tokenized stocks a five-year exemption
The SEC issued an order granting tokenized securities trading venues (TSVS) a five-year interim conditional exemption, letting them trade tokenized NMS stocks through permissioned AMMs and liquidity pools without registering as exchanges, and giving liquidity providers a limited market-maker exemption. Two key conditions: token holders must get the same rights as holders of the underlying stock, such as dividends and voting; and third-party tokenization requires written notice with an opportunity for the issuer to object. Santi read that out and said this clause could directly break the current onchain tokenized stock play — if AMC can object, you can't just throw AMC onto Hyperliquid. Rob said this is almost certainly coming, because onchain tokenized stocks currently create strange dislocations after hours and pre-market, and Robinhood pairing memecoins with tokenized stocks is an example.

22:43 The winner in tokenization is the whole ecosystem
Rob said it's hard to point to a single winner. The obvious beneficiaries are issuers, existing exchanges and clearinghouses, new exchanges that want into the US market (Coinbase, Polymarket, Lighter, Hyperliquid, Backpack), global neobanks, and new transfer agents and core infrastructure providers like Alpaca. Santi said his first reaction was Superstate and Securitize, and Securitize rose 16% that day. Rob said this looks more like a rising tide lifting all boats than value concentrating in one place. He added that as more assets come onchain, everything onchain gets bigger — more liquidity, more users, better infrastructure, more stablecoin issuance.

29:06 S&P buying Open Zeppelin is buying data
S&P is a ratings agency with a roughly $120 billion market cap and about $14 billion in revenue. This week it first led Kao's Series B extension (Kao raised its B round four years ago; this time it may have raised about $50 million, bringing the B round to about $110 million, with investors including RBC, DRW, Broadridge, BNP and Nasdaq), then acquired smart contract security firm Open Zeppelin. Rob said the acquisition surprised him — Open Zeppelin doesn't seem like a company that would run a process to sell itself. His read: S&P issues ratings, and it can use Open Zeppelin for real-time risk benchmarks and data, to assess what's happening inside protocols, and then sell that to clients. Santi said he heard this is the first such deal, and that traditional capital markets data and analytics players (Moody's and others) will do more like it. Rob said many crypto companies raised a lot of money and have good products but aren't good enough as standalone businesses, and companies like S&P grow into conglomerates by continually buying good niche products and then bundling them for you through a terminal.

37:40 Circle pushing memes on Arc's first day was a misstep
Circle launched Arc with more than 190 partners on day one and over $220 million of pre-seeded TVL in a Morpho vault. Rob said he doesn't understand why Circle came out pushing a bunch of memes on day one, since Arc had always been positioned as a payments-first chain, talking about agentic finance, privacy, FX liquidity and real commercial activity. He said this is the exact opposite of the story Circle has long told, and it left a lot of people with a bad impression. Santi said he went to Circle's launch event yesterday, and the room and Twitter were two completely different worlds — within an hour he met people from BlackRock, DTCC, ICE, Visa and MoneyGram, and Circle's convening power is enormous; if it had launched purely on its original positioning, it would have gone over much better. Rob said Circle may have seen Robinhood chain's success, but Robinhood is a trading platform and Circle is a payments company — having bought Taza Pay, it should stay in its own lane.

42:38 Circle's revenue gets cut in half by rates
Rob said he doesn't expect 4% to 4.5% rates to last forever, and that rates will normalize to between 2% and 3%, which means that if Circle is purely an interest-income business, its revenue at current TVL gets cut in half. He also said that as a payments stablecoin, if you can't share yield with end customers, there isn't much reason to hold large amounts of it. Circle's agreement with Coinbase requires giving 50% to Coinbase, which puts it at a disadvantage competing with new stablecoins. So Circle is trying to become a payments company and get a payments company's multiple, and Arc and the Circle Payment Network are both part of that story. Santi said don't underestimate USDC's network effect — in DeFi there is now only one thing that matters for liquidity, and that's USDC; every DeFi founder needs USDC on their platform.

46:14 Instinct's reckoning comes in month four
Rob said companies are now getting bigger faster and raising more faster, that venture capital as a market structure is broken, and that the hottest companies see valuations rise faster and faster regardless of fundamentals. He said a company's first big reckoning usually comes in year four, but Instinct's first big reckoning will come in month four — because the two biggest companies in the world are about to ship direct competitors, Grokbot and Meta's Muse. Santi said in his own use Muse is six to eight times better than Instinct; Instinct is clearly compute-constrained, and for the same question Muse is sometimes 10 to 15 minutes faster, fails less often, and can route around the roadblocks Resy has set up for these products. Rob said he doesn't know how growth investors are comfortable at this valuation, and the only thing that could prove them wrong is Instinct sprinting to train its own model — but that takes a billion dollars to build data centers.

item.title: Prediction Markets Aren't Casinos, but 90% of the Volume Is Sports
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.description: Kalshi spent four years on compliance to win 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a sportsbook's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.
item.content:encoded:
Kalshi spent four years on compliance to win 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a sportsbook's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.

The first half is founder narrative; the value is in the middle and back: how contracts are written, sports at 90%, regulatory risk. Worth listening for anyone who wants to understand the mechanics of prediction markets.

8:16 Four years of compliance first, then the first market
Kalshi's two founders wrote "regulatory first" into the company's principles and spent four years getting regulatory approval before launching their first market. Mansoor calls this anti-Silicon Valley: everyone else builds the product and patches in compliance later, while they went to the federal government first and asked how this thing should be regulated. The cost was that for the first four years they thought about quitting almost every day, held together by the fact that the cost of regret was too high. The payoff came in 2024, when a federal appeals court ruled Kalshi could list election contracts, landing before the presidential election. Mansoor attributes the 90% market share directly to that path: institutions would rather plug into a platform inside the system, because changing the rules from outside the system is harder.

15:36 Prediction markets force you to shut up, not to take a position
Robin Hanson lays out three mechanisms that make prediction markets more accurate than polls or expert interviews. First, people being interviewed have an incentive to be interesting, dramatic and to tell the questioner what they want to hear, while the market only rewards being right. Second, the market gives you an incentive to shut up about things you don't understand — you only bet in the few markets where you genuinely have an edge, whereas interviewees will answer confidently on anything. Third, the market doesn't require you to have a direct view on a topic; it invites you to find the biases and errors in other people's pricing, and if you find one, it pays you to correct it. He closes with the old poker-table line: sit down, look for the sucker, and if you can't find him, the sucker is you — so don't play that market.

20:48 Internal prediction markets die on the project owner's excuse
Eli Lilly ran an internal prediction market in the early 2000s that successfully predicted which drug compounds would pass Phase III trials; Google ran one called Google Profit. Both were considered effective, and neither survived. Hanson's explanation: the project owner wants to know whether they'll deliver on time, but what they want even more is a good excuse if they fail. And the best excuse is precisely "everything was going fine and then at the last minute something nobody could have foreseen happened." A market that keeps accurately predicting whether you'll be late voids that excuse in advance, so nobody wants it to exist.

22:58 Domain expertise is not the key skill for forecasting the future
Mansoor cites Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting research: put experts in a given domain — geopolitics, say — up against a group of non-experts forecasting the same set of events, and the non-experts win. His explanation is that domain experts become too doctrinaire over time, while people who can step back and look at a problem coolly are better calibrated and less biased. Mansoor says this is a fairly heretical claim in politics, academia and financial analysis — it implies that if you want a more accurate answer, you should look for a diverse group of participants who pride themselves on self-calibration, critical reading and filtering information, not an authority in some field. He treats this as Kalshi's underlying logic.

33:28 One contract takes a month to write, for grammar and apostrophes
Nicole Kagan writes the contracts and self-certifies them with the CFTC. The most complex category is "what someone will say in a given speech," and they recently rewrote the rules because a pile of grammar questions came up: what if there's an apostrophe? If the person misspeaks or mispronounces it, does it still count as the same word? What if it appears inside a proper noun? What if the livestream cuts out midway and the video is uploaded somewhere else later? Those rules took more than a month to write, run seven or eight pages, and are extremely detailed. When Bloomberg reported on them, it guessed the rules were built for automated processing and must be for AI; Kagan says that's not it at all — they wrote them so users could understand, and never considered that anything a human can parse a computer probably can too.

35:35 When you can't call it, settle at the last fair price
Kalshi's contracts are usually binary: pay $1 if the event happens, $0 if it doesn't, with every position fully collateralized — if one side stakes 30 cents, someone must stake 70. But some cases can't be judged yes or no. Cardi B was visibly dancing during her seven-second Super Bowl halftime cameo, but she had no mic and there was no way to confirm whether she was singing, so the team said they were "epistemically uncertain" and settled at the last fair price. Another case is 50-50: when multiple people win simultaneously, each settles at 50 cents. Kagan says they have the right to do this when it's genuinely unclear whether an event meets the criteria, and they've already revised the halftime contract — the new rules require an audible lead or backing vocal, and under them Cardi B did not perform.

41:52 Ninety percent of volume is sports, and that's the most uncomfortable fact
Dubner puts it directly: roughly 90% of Kalshi's volume is concentrated in a category barely mentioned until then — sports, the business that makes DraftKings and FanDuel nervous. Mansoor's response is that sports' share is falling fast as other categories grow faster, but he concedes that "10% is also a lot, and don't forget we're big." He insists on distinguishing gambling from trading: all derivatives markets are mostly speculative, speculation provides liquidity, and the key isn't whether speculation exists but the business model — one model hunts for losers and bans winners, the other pursues price discovery and wants smart people in. He also concedes the second model carries risk, saying there is "responsible gambling" and "responsible trading," and that platforms have a duty to monitor.

44:00 Seventy to eighty percent of active users never place a trade
Mansoor says one of his favorite numbers is that 70% to 80% of active users don't trade — they just log in every day, keep it next to X and a couple of newspapers, and use it to calibrate or check information. Kalshi's business model is a neutral platform, like the NYSE or Nasdaq, taking an average 1% on trades and not caring who wins or loses. He also says the information environment is getting more polarized and the signal-to-noise ratio is falling, because social media algorithms reward clickbait: a nuanced, restrained, multi-paragraph take gets four likes on X, while something wildly outrageous gets tens of thousands; prediction markets have exactly the opposite incentive — the nuanced, boring, well-calibrated judgment is the one that makes money.

item.title: Diffusion Isn't Just for Images — It's Going to Win at Language Model Inference
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.description: Autoregressive inference has to generate one token at a time, sequentially, and it's a memory-bandwidth bottleneck; diffusion models process many tokens in parallel at once, and the inference workload looks more like training — that's why Inception is betting on it.
item.content:encoded:
Autoregressive inference has to generate one token at a time, sequentially, and it's a memory-bandwidth bottleneck; diffusion models process many tokens in parallel at once, and the inference workload looks more like training — that's why Inception is betting on it.

A diffusion model founder explains clearly why parallelism at the inference stage becomes the architectural deciding factor, and how a 50-person company finds differentiation in the gap between giants.

3:10 Diffusion models started because GANs were too unstable
Ermon says that back when he was working on image generation he was very dissatisfied with GANs: they worked, but training was extremely unstable and results were hard to reproduce. So in 2019 he and his PhD students turned to score-based generative models, with the idea of training a neural network to denoise — if it can denoise, that means it understands image structure, and it can then work in reverse to progressively refine a clean image out of pure noise. This is the underlying technology of modern diffusion models. He stresses that today's best image, video, some music, and a large number of protein models are all based on diffusion.

5:11 The 2024 paper moved diffusion onto text
Ermon's team published a paper in 2024 that, for the first time, got a diffusion model to match autoregressive model quality at GPT-2 scale (under a billion parameters): the same perplexity, the same degree of data fit, but roughly 10x faster generation, because diffusion outputs multiple tokens at once. He says this was still fairly academic, but it was enough to make him decide to start a company and scale the technology to commercial scale.

8:14 Autoregressive inference is a memory-bandwidth bottleneck
Ermon analogises the 2017 switch from RNNs to transformers to the inference stage: during training, transformers won by processing multiple tokens in parallel, but at inference time autoregressive models are still sequential — before generating the 10th token you must first generate all the tokens before it. This workload is extremely memory-bandwidth-bound; most of the time is spent moving weights between levels of the memory hierarchy, with very little arithmetic, which is unfriendly to GPUs. Diffusion models' inference workload looks more like training — processing multiple tokens in parallel at once — so it naturally matches the compute pattern GPUs are good at.

10:16 Inference efficiency also caps RL post-training
Ermon points out that economics are determined by how much intelligence you get per watt and per dollar. A great deal of progress in reasoning models comes from test-time compute scaling, and one of the bottlenecks in RL post-training is generating rollouts — letting the model explore, scoring trajectories, then improving the model. So inference efficiency directly gates post-training efficiency: a model that scales better at inference time will automatically also scale better at post-training time. This is the core logic behind his bet on diffusion LLMs, and behind his claim that ‘the more parallel approach will eventually win’.

12:19 Mercury is benchmarked against Haiku, Flash, and the mini series
Ermon says Inception's Mercury model is benchmarked against speed-optimised models like Haiku, Flash, and mini nano, with comparable quality but significantly faster, and it is already serving customers in production. He stresses that you cannot just run a diffusion LLM on vLLM or SGLang — you have to build your own serving engine to handle the complexity of real production workloads. This is both a barrier and a moat: even if someone else trains a diffusion LLM, without a corresponding serving engine they can't put it to use.

17:21 A voice customer switched from custom chips back to Nvidia GPUs
Ermon gives the example of voice agent company OpenCall: the voice pipeline includes ASR, an inference LLM for tool calling, and TTS, and speed is critical. OpenCall originally served its LLM on Cerebras custom chips to reach the required speed, then switched to Inception's diffusion LLM, because it could get equivalent speed on Nvidia GPUs — higher availability, lower cost, better quality. Ermon says once you get used to a fast model you can't go back, like broadband.

25:26 Diffusion models are inherently easier to control than autoregressive ones
Ermon says diffusion models are generally easier to control than autoregressive models: with autoregressive you have to wait until the entire object is generated before you know whether it satisfies constraints, whether it's aligned, what score a reward function gives it; diffusion is coarse-to-fine generation, so from early on you can tell whether the direction is right, and you can use external reward functions or constraint sets to guide generation. There is a fair amount of evidence in the academic literature supporting this, and some guidance methods simply can't be done on autoregressive models at all. He sees this as the differentiation space for future product experiences.

29:29 20% to 30% of tasks are extremely latency-sensitive
Ermon estimates, referencing OpenRouter's task categories (research, chat, coding, software engineering, log processing, etc.), that roughly 20% to 30% of those tasks care a great deal about latency. As a lower bound, that share of the workload can be served by whichever model offers the highest quality within a given latency budget. He also acknowledges that we are not yet at frontier intelligence, and much of the workload still needs frontier-level intelligence, so the addressable market for diffusion models is layered.

item.title: When Your Kids Fight, Be a Witness, Not a Judge
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-当证人别当法官/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-当证人别当法官/
item.description: Fairness is not equality: give each child what they need, not the identical thing. A parent's job is not to rule on who was right, but to describe what happened and let them find the next step.
item.content:encoded:
Fairness is not equality: give each child what they need, not the identical thing. A parent's job is not to rule on who was right, but to describe what happened and let them find the next step.

Medium information density, but three frameworks — "witness, not judge," "fairness is not equality," and "forced apology is not repair" — are concrete and actionable, well suited to parents with more than one child.

3:05 Deal with your own sibling baggage first
The episode opens by saying: before you intervene, sort out your own emotions. Everyone carries sibling baggage — even people without siblings carry a longing for that relationship, or relief at not having it. The fairness trap is what most easily sets parents off: a piece of cake, a looser rule, a new dress from childhood all leave behind a memory of "I got cheated." Those feelings get called up when you step into your kids' conflict. So the core instruction is: you are a witness, not a judge. The moment you start ruling, the judgment comes from your own history, not from the two children in front of you.

5:07 When you must step in: danger, power imbalance, deadlock
There are three criteria: if a child is in danger, step in; if there's a power imbalance, step in; if they're stuck in a deadlock, step in. If the two are evenly matched and both safe, you can step back and occasionally ask, "Is everyone okay?" What deserves special vigilance is when power dynamics turn into toxic bullying — this is rare, but when it happens, an adult must cut it off. The episode stresses that children who are bullied by peers or siblings have significantly worse outcomes as adults, and the damage is far more serious than we realize. But bullying has a strict definition: a power difference, repetition, malice, intentional abuse. Merely being "annoying" doesn't count.

6:07 Intervene in sportscaster mode, don't ask who started it
If you have to step in, use "sportscaster mode": like a commentator, describe only the facts you saw — "I noticed this happened over here, did I get that right?" This validates both children at once, takes no side, and produces no winner. Questions to avoid include "Who started it," "Why are you always like this," and "There's just something wrong with you." The episode draws a key distinction: telling a child "what you did was inconsiderate" and telling a child "you're stupid" are two different things. The latter attacks a person's worth and gets a child to bind their anger and emotional outbursts to "I'm not worth anything as a person." The moment you hear dehumanizing language, even mid-screaming-match, pause it on the spot and require a different way of saying it.

9:13 Under two, protect the little one without making the big one hate him
Under two, you only need to protect the younger one, while trying not to alienate the older one. The older child is already processing "the baby stole my attention," and then gets told "this is your best friend, don't you love him?" — what he's thinking is "No, I don't love him," but sometimes he does. So tell him plainly: you can be angry at your sibling and love him deeply at the same time, you can dislike him today and still love him very much — these are mixed feelings, and they're completely normal. Also explain: protecting the little one's body is the adult's job, because he can't get out of the way himself, so sometimes I'll pick him up and carry him off. That kind of intervention doesn't heighten the tension, and it isn't saying who's better or worse — only who needs protection from real danger.

14:28 Fairness is not equality — it's giving each child what they need
The most useful item in prevention mode: fairness is not equality — not equality, but equity. You give each child what they need, not the identical thing. The episode gives a concrete example: giving two children peanut butter cupcakes the same size, same recipe, same flavor looks perfectly equal, but one of them is allergic to peanuts — so it isn't fair. You can give him vanilla, making sure both children have cake, but not the same cake. This framework applies directly to challenges like "Why does my sister get a phone at twelve and I don't": you are different people, I learned more later, so I made a different decision.

16:31 Don't label your kids — labels follow them for life
A shared label for all the children can promote good behavior — telling your kids "you're helpers" produces more helping behavior. But if you give the "helper" label to only one child in the house, it creates tension and a problematic dynamic. The episode says labeling builds a dynamic that, to put it dramatically, "clings to them." Teachers, friends, other people's parents, relatives will all label them, so a parent's job is to offset that damage, because labels bring resentment, insecurity, lack of motivation, and tension between siblings that needn't be as distant as it becomes.

18:41 Forced apology is not repair — it's fake repair
Repair doesn't require a formal apology. Kids who are fighting suddenly giggle together, share an inside joke, make faces at each other — that is repair, that is reconnecting, and you are watching it happen. Every reconnection reinforces the relationship, telling them this foundation is permanent, it will get messy, but we always come back. But if you feel you must force an apology, the episode is explicit: an apology is not repair unless it genuinely comes from the heart, from really feeling you did wrong and wanting to make it up to the other person. Saying "I'm sorry" and saying "apologize to your brother" are neither one what the scientific literature calls repair. Fake repair can't build a strong foundation. What you can ask is: "How do you think that made your sibling feel? What could you do to make him feel better?" If the child says nothing, you don't just drop it — you come back and ask again a little later.

23:55 Be curious about the kid who starts it, don't just punish
When one child really is repeatedly provoking, first let the other children know you see it: "I've noticed your sister has started it the last few times, and I also see how hard you're trying not to fight back — that's hard, let's keep practicing." With the provoking child, get genuinely curious first: why is he provoking so often? Does he need more one-on-one time? Is there some longing, jealousy or need you haven't noticed? Try to meet it without depriving the other children. If you just yell "you always start it" and punish, you don't teach him the underlying skill, and you don't teach him self-reflection — "Why do I keep starting this? What do I actually want?" Teaching a child to figure out what he wants and get it in a productive way is one of the most important things there is. Going after it by provoking loses most of the time.

item.title: America's Richest Are Hiding in Small Business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-oddlots-美国最富的一群人-藏在小生意里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-oddlots-美国最富的一群人-藏在小生意里/
item.description: Half of the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income, and the owners of these businesses aren't tech giants — they're car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.
item.content:encoded:
Half of the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income, and the owners of these businesses aren't tech giants — they're car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.

A new study built on linked IRS full tax-return data pulls the question of "who are the rich" away from the tech narrative and back to regional middle-market businesses; high information density, suited to anyone tracking taxes, PE and wealth distribution.

6:13 Tax returns assemble a different picture of the rich
More than a decade ago, the two authors were commissioned by the Treasury to link corporate tax returns with the returns of owners and employees, because even the IRS couldn't match the different forms belonging to the same business. They found that the picture of the rich painted by the media and by Capital in the Twenty-First Century is very different from the actual picture in US tax returns: not passive rent-collecting Gilded Age monopolists, but millions of actively operating middle-market regional business owners. This data project later became the basis of the book.

12:16 Seventy percent of pass-through income flows to the top 1%
Of pass-through business income, 70 cents of every dollar flows to the top 1% of earners. From the 1980s to 2021, more than half of the growth in the top 1%'s income share came from pass-through business income. So anyone trying to understand income inequality and wealth inequality cannot get around this sector. The authors originally assumed monopolistic giants were passively collecting the money, but found instead middle-market regional businesses spread across the whole country, numbering in the millions.

15:22 Car dealers are the single biggest bucket of pass-through income
The book opens with a "wedding of the century": a third-generation Mercedes dealer in Florida threw his daughter's wedding in Paris, rented out Versailles for the dinner, and spent $60 million — right after selling the dealership for several hundred million dollars. When the authors looked at pass-through income of the top 0.1% by industry, car dealers ranked first. They then went to yacht and private jet registration data and found these people by name, because tax returns themselves cannot identify individuals.

19:23 Car dealer wealth is half skill, half licence
The authors tell two stories. Larry Miller started in Toyota's parts division, took the parts business from 961st to first, later owned more than 40 dealerships and bought the Utah Jazz — a good case of "move slow and make things." But the other side is regulatory protection: franchise laws were meant to protect small dealers from being force-fed inventory by Ford and GM, yet in 2008 Chrysler had three times as many dealerships as Toyota while selling the same number of cars, and closing a store meant paying three years' rent. Dealers also enjoy geographic monopolies and high margins on add-on services like warranties and financing.

22:25 Beer distributors are a rent-collecting layer left by Prohibition
When you see a truck on the road with Budweiser on it, the truck actually belongs to a distributor, such as Reyes. These distributors sit between brewers and bars, restaurants and grocery stores; state laws require beer to pass through this layer, originally to stop big brewers from controlling production and distribution at the same time. The result is that these "little guys" became big guys, showing up en masse in the private jet data. The authors mention a beer wholesalers' convention in San Antonio where the mayor said he had never seen so many private jets at the airport.

34:31 Same anaesthesiologist, far higher tax burden for the employee
The book compares two anaesthesiologists: one runs a private practice through an S-Corp, the other draws a salary from a hospital system. The former treats most of his income as business profit, pays no payroll tax and no uncapped Medicare surtax, even though he bills Medicare heavily. The IRS only requires payroll tax on the "reasonable compensation" portion of wages; anything above that counts as profit. The 2017 reform cut the top pass-through rate from 37% to below 30%, and although it put guardrails on professional services like doctors, by spinning out surgery, ancillary services or real estate, more income can still be shifted into the lower-rate bucket.

38:35 A quarter of federal elected officials are pass-through owners too
The authors say the reason the tax loophole survives so long is that roughly a quarter of federal elected officials are themselves pass-through business owners. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno is a car dealer, and the Social Security plan he introduced with Elizabeth Warren is funded by a payroll tax on working-class wages, with no mention at all of these wealthy business owners. The authors argue the most realistic reform is not to abolish the loophole but to cap it by income: for instance, business income above $1 million or $400,000 would no longer qualify for the deduction that cuts the rate from 37% to 30%.

48:52 The owners' share of the pie rose from four-tenths to five-tenths
Over the past 25 years, 60% of growth in the corporate sector came from the pass-through form, so the pie is getting bigger; at the same time, the share owners take out of the pie rose from a third to 40% to about 50%. Using data from 2001 to 2021, the authors calculate: value added per worker rose from $34,000 to $52,000, a gain of $18,000, of which owners took $15,000. They attribute this to skill scarcity (the US has 30% fewer doctors per capita than the OECD average, with the AMA restricting supply), policy-created scarcity, and the rising value of professional services such as M&A.

item.title: Hair relaxer made Black women beautiful, and made them pay with their health
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ninepi-直发剂让黑人女性变美-也让她们付出健康代价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ninepi-直发剂让黑人女性变美-也让她们付出健康代价/
item.description: Chemical hair relaxer built the Black community's earliest millionaire industry and has also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is both an economic ladder and a bodily cost.
item.content:encoded:
Chemical hair relaxer built the Black community's earliest millionaire industry and has also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is both an economic ladder and a bodily cost.

This episode has medium information density, but it tells the story of how one product can be empowerment and harm at the same time, very concretely — suited to listeners interested in consumer history, public health, and the racial economy.

1:06 Hair relaxer is "creamy crack"
Chemical hair relaxer has a nickname in the salon: creamy crack, because it is addictive like cocaine — once you start, it is very hard to stop. When you stop, the new curly growth breaks off where it meets the already-straightened dead hair. The week before use you cannot wash your hair or scratch your scalp, or you will get burned; when applying it you have to avoid the scalp and coat only the hair shaft, but leaving it too long near the ends still stings. In the episode the host recalls being slathered with relaxer for the first time at age 9, having already seen women in the salon cry out in pain.

5:18 From African hair tradition to a survival strategy
Hair historian Lorie Tharps says starting the story from slavery is starting from chapter two and missing chapter one: Africa already had a rich hair tradition, and hair connected tribe, family, and identity. After being enslaved in America, straightening went from self-expression to survival strategy — because they were told their hair was inferior, ugly, more like an animal's, and straightening became a visual way to prove "we are equal to you." They used butter instead of palm oil, made shampoo from cornmeal and kerosene, used butter knives as crude curling irons, and wrapped hair in yarn to straighten it.

8:21 Barbers' money built Black colleges
The methods these enslaved people invented were good enough to make them the first choice as barbers and wig makers for white people. White people paid for their craft, and this channel let many of them buy their own freedom. Tharps says some early Black colleges and institutions were funded or founded by Black barbers, such as Wilberforce University — an HBCU entirely owned and operated by African Americans, built in large part on barbering income. But the irony is that these Black barbers did not cut Black people's hair at the time; they served white clients.

10:22 The hot comb gave way to an accidental discovery
Madame CJ Walker and Annie Turnbo Malone used the hot comb plus hair oil to produce sleek straight hair, turning scattered straightening methods into a system, and Walker thereby became the first self-made millionaire woman in America, of any race. But the hot comb's effect was temporary — sweat, humidity, or rain restored the original state. In the early 1900s, Cleveland tailor Garrett Augustus Morgan wanted to invent a substance that kept high-speed machines and needles from damaging wool and other animal fur, and after trying a formula he found the fur had straightened. He first tested it on a neighbor's dog, then on his own hair, and both straightened — he had accidentally discovered that lye (sodium hydroxide) plus other things could straighten hair.

14:24 The man who put relaxer on drugstore shelves
George Johnson is called by Tharps the Madam CJ Walker of his era. A barber who made homemade conk came to this chemist and asked whether he could make something fast and easy, and so came Ultra Wave for men, followed by Ultra Sheen for women. Unlike the temporary hot comb and dangerous homemade lye formulas, Ultra Sheen was long-lasting, safer, and available at any drugstore, with no need to go to a salon. That privacy was crucial: straightening hair with chemicals carried shame, and doing it at home meant no one saw you going to the salon.

16:26 Profits flowed back to the Black community, then regulators took aim
Johnson put profits back into the Black community: Soul Train, Essence Magazine, Chicago's Independence Bank — then the largest Black-owned bank in the country, lending to homeowners and entrepreneurs redlined by white banks; funding Martin Luther King Jr. and Jesse Jackson; employing hundreds of Black and brown workers who could not find jobs because of racial discrimination, giving them profit sharing, full health insurance, on-site nurses, full college tuition, paid maternity and sick leave, and four-day weekends every holiday. In 1964 Johnson Products became the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange. But in 1975 the FTC required Johnson to put a warning label on the outside of relaxer packaging saying the product contained lye and could be harmful — while Revlon's relaxer, which also contained lye, was not immediately required to add a label, and the delay ran nearly two years.

20:28 The civil rights movement flipped the politics of straight hair
During the Black Power era, Black people decided straight hair had solved nothing — from Madam CJ Walker's straightening comb to relaxer, every method had been tried, and it still had not worked. So came a simpler and more radical idea: I will no longer straighten my hair, I will use my hair as protest. Black hair grows up and out, and does not make you smaller — it makes you taller. The political flip was so complete that some Black people with naturally straight hair got perms, because not everyone's hair can grow into an Angela Davis-style afro. But the beauty industry then commodified the afro, selling wigs and marketing it as beauty and empowerment while also defanging it, turning it into just another fashion trend. By the 1980s, straight hair was back.

28:38 A 34,000-woman study: two and a half times the risk
A large 2022 study followed 34,000 women and found that frequent users of chemical hair straightening products — most of them Black women — were two and a half times as likely to develop uterine cancer as never-users. New York Times Magazine contributor Linda Varosa says this was the first high-quality study to link straightening products, Black women, and two cancers (endometrial cancer and uterine cancer). The study also linked these products to fibroids, and Black women have fibroids at far higher rates than other women. The study shows correlation, not causation, but Tharps thinks agonizing over correlation versus causation misses the point: she thinks the red flag should be waved directly, with warnings on packaging, labels, and in salons.

item.title: A Broken Arm Forced a Perfect French Score: Constraints Are the Engine of Creativity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-cautionary-断臂逼出的法语满分-限制才是创造力的引擎/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-cautionary-断臂逼出的法语满分-限制才是创造力的引擎/
item.description: After David Epstein broke his arm, he was forced to replace note-taking with image-based memory, and his French scores went to perfect. During a two-day London Underground strike, many people found better commutes. Constraints are not obstacles; they are the switch that forces you to experiment.
item.content:encoded:
After David Epstein broke his arm, he was forced to replace note-taking with image-based memory, and his French scores went to perfect. During a two-day London Underground strike, many people found better commutes. Constraints are not obstacles; they are the switch that forces you to experiment.

Medium information density. The core is the framework distinguishing useful constraints from useless ones. The second half — scientific integrity and entrepreneurial experimentation — is worth more than the first half.

5:28 A broken arm forced a memory method into existence
In eighth grade, playing American football, David Epstein threw too hard and his arm snapped on the follow-through; his right arm was bound from shoulder to hand against his torso. His French class had a weekly dictation test: listen to a native speaker's recording and fill in the blanks in a text. He was mediocre. With his right hand bound, he couldn't write fast enough with his left, so he had to hold the flying words in his head first, linking each word to something sports-related — he didn't know at the time that this was called a mnemonic device. As a result he could remember every word, then slowly fill them in with his left hand, and started getting perfect scores. The key mechanism: his most convenient path was blocked, forcing him to find an alternative, and the alternative was better.

8:35 A two-day subway strike improved commutes for years
During a London Underground strike, people were forced to find different routes to work. The strike lasted only 48 hours, but a substantial share of people discovered a better commute than the one they had used for weeks, months or even years, and kept using it afterward. Epstein recalls the study saying this collectively saved about 1,500 hours of commuting per day. His inference: we normally experiment too little; useful constraints drive people to run experiments they otherwise wouldn't, and the payoff from those experiments can far exceed the inconvenience.

10:38 General Magic died from too many resources
General Magic was a startup of the late 1980s and early 1990s with nearly unlimited talent, money and resources, and it judged the direction of technology for the coming decades correctly — on paper, they invented the iPhone. But Epstein says more startups die of indigestion than of starvation: because they could do anything, they did everything, and projects kept expanding out of control. They never clearly defined who the customer was (the so-called Joe Sixpack — nobody knew who that was), and ended up building for each other rather than solving a specific problem. Internally, a low-level service engineer built a prototype of eBay and handed it to the company, and it was rejected as "too small, can't become anything." Epstein argues they should have started from smaller goals and smaller milestones.

12:41 A world without constraints is a fiction
Tim Harford raises a disagreement: General Magic wasn't without constraints, it's just that all its constraints were long-term, so they could pretend the constraints didn't exist until the money and time actually ran out. Epstein partly agrees but corrects him: they didn't lack money — they had more than they could spend — what they lacked was time. He cites Oliver Burkeman's view: believing that with the right productivity tools you can get everything done may just be a refusal to face your own mortality, a refusal to prioritize ruthlessly. About two-thirds of the former General Magic employees he interviewed said they simply couldn't figure out what not to do. Epstein treats this as a parable for the AI era: when the cost of starting something approaches zero, it removes the hard work of deciding what not to do, which may be one reason adoption has risen unprecedentedly while productivity hasn't risen correspondingly.

14:42 The Hemingway principle fights the sense of urgency
Epstein calls his own writing method the Hemingway principle: Hemingway stopped mid-sentence, so that the next day he knew which important place to return to. The last thing Epstein does at the end of each workday is designate which important place to start from the next day. He says this guards against the two main ways a workday goes off the rails: first, falling into an algorithmic feed or inbox first thing in the morning; second, the so-called mere urgency effect — people prioritize what feels urgent (like answering email) over what is truly important, even when the important thing objectively deserves more time.

17:44 Pre-registration makes miracle drugs disappear
Before 2000, psychology was full of counterintuitive findings: thinking of Florida makes you walk more slowly, power poses raise testosterone, hurricanes with female names are more dangerous. Medicine was the same — almost every NIH-funded cardiovascular drug trial found a positive result; after 2000, new trials were almost all negative. The turning point was the NIH forcing researchers to constrain their behavior: write down your prediction in advance and stick to it. Epstein explains the mechanism: researchers would first make a prediction, and when it didn't hold, they would dig through a large dataset for a correlation, then retroactively invent a prediction, so that at publication it looked as if they had been looking for this from the start. Digging through data amounts to running nearly infinite tests, and each test raises the probability of a false positive, so a false-positive association is almost guaranteed.

20:45 Everything in the fridge both causes and prevents cancer
Epstein's favorite "dark humor paper" aggregated all nutrition research and found that almost every food you can think of has been shown in different studies to both cause and prevent cancer — with the exception of bacon, which was only found to cause cancer. He also tells the case of nutrition star researcher Brian Woznick: he did the famous bottomless soup bowl experiment, where people ate far more when an unseen tube kept refilling their bowls. Later he wrote a blog post describing his research method: when a prediction didn't hold, he handed the data to a graduate student and said "find me something positive," and she never failed. Epstein's analogy: it's like firing randomly at a wall, then finding the dense cluster of bullet holes and painting a bullseye and a ten-ring around it, and passersby marvel at the marksmanship. Most of Woznick's life's work was eventually retracted, and his research had been cited in a Nobel laureate's book.

27:51 Entrepreneurs who write predictions fail more but succeed more
Epstein extends pre-registration to personal life: when making a behavior change (say, wanting to exercise more), first write down what you plan to try and what you predict it will produce, then do it, then check whether the prediction came true — this educates your intuition. He cites a randomized controlled study: entrepreneurs were randomly assigned to a "scientific method training" group or an ordinary market research group; those trained falsified their own prior beliefs more often, discovering that the value they thought they were adding to the market didn't hold, and as a result they pivoted more often and succeeded more often.
